       direct Parliament to criminalise the online publication of misinformation that endangers
       public health. The petitioner argued that a legislative vacuum existed because existing


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                          36


     laws inadequately addressed the specific medium and harm involved. What is the most
     defensible judicial response?
options:
The Court must issue the directions sought because the existence of a demonstrable
      public health emergency overrides the separation of powers in exceptional situations,
      empowering the Court to legislate by judicial direction when Parliament has failed to
      act.

The Court should decline to issue directions mandating Parliament to criminalise
      specific conduct, because the creation of criminal offences lies within Parliament's
      exclusive domain under the constitutional scheme, and the absence of a specific statute
      does not constitute a vacancy that justifies judicial lawmaking.

The Court should issue interim directions treating the online publication of health
      misinformation as a criminal offence by necessary implication, pending enactment of
      suitable legislation, to prevent an imminent threat to life under Article 21.

The Court must refer the matter to the Law Commission of India with a time-bound
      direction to submit a draft legislation, since directing Parliament to legislate is
      impermissible but directing an advisory body to recommend legislation falls within the
      Court's supervisory jurisdiction.

A High Court issued a detailed set of guidelines directing employers to constitute
     committees, mandating the reporting of communal incidents at workplaces, and
     prescribing penalties for non-compliance. The Court relied on a prior Supreme Court
     precedent in which judicial directions were issued in the absence of legislation on
     workplace sexual harassment. The employer challenged the guidelines. What principle
     determines the validity of the guidelines?

The guidelines are valid in their entirety because a High Court exercising jurisdiction
      under Article 226 has inherent authority to fill gaps in existing law whenever
      constitutional rights are at stake, regardless of whether the gap arises from total
      legislative silence or inadequate enforcement.

The guidelines are valid only if there is a complete legislative vacuum on the specific
      subject matter addressed, since the precedent allowing judicial directions in lieu of
      legislation applies exclusively to situations of total statutory absence, not to situations

      go beyond its specific provisions.

      compliance obligations on private employers constitutes a legislative act that only
      Parliament may authorise, making the High Court's intervention unconstitutional
      regardless of the statutory context.

Parliament enacted a statute defining certain categories of 'hate content' and
     criminalising them. A petitioner challenged the statute on the ground that the definition
     of hate content was vague and overbroad, potentially criminalising legitimate dissent.
     The Supreme Court agreed that the definition required tightening. What remedial action
     is available to the Court?
options:
The Court may rewrite the statutory definition to make it clearer and narrower,
      prescribing a judicially crafted text that Parliament must adopt, on the ground that the
      constitutional obligation to protect free speech authorises the Court to substitute its own
      drafting for Parliament's imprecision.

The Court may read down the provision to exclude legitimate expression from its ambit,
      strike down the overbroad portion if it is severable without destroying the legislative
      intent, but cannot substitute its own text for the void provision or direct Parliament to
      enact specific replacement language.

The Court must immediately strike down the entire statute rather than reading it down,
      because a criminal statute with a vague definition of the prohibited conduct cannot be
      partially saved; the rule of strict construction in criminal law requires all-or-nothing
      adjudication.

The Court may direct the Ministry of Home Affairs to issue an executive notification
      clarifying the scope of the statute in lieu of legislative amendment, since executive
      clarification of criminal statutes through subordinate legislation is within the Court's
      power to direct under Article 142.

The Supreme Court received a petition pointing out that existing laws on promoting
     enmity between groups were rarely enforced by state police forces. The petitioner
     argued that judicial directions compelling enforcement were constitutionally distinct
     from creating new offences and therefore permissible. Does this distinction hold?


                                  12minutestoclat.com                                         38
options:
The distinction holds in full, and the Court may issue specific directions mandating law
      enforcement authorities to register cases and investigate complaints under existing
      statutory provisions, since enforcing existing law is categorically different from making
      new law.

The distinction does not hold here, because directing enforcement of criminal statutes
      at the initiative of a court, rather than in response to specific complaints, encroaches
      upon the State's executive discretion in law enforcement, which is part of the separation

The distinction holds only with respect to non-discretionary ministerial acts;

      directions for ongoing enforcement across all future cases would amount to a standing

The distinction holds in principle, but a court may only direct enforcement where the
      petitioner demonstrates that a specific cognisable offence has been committed and a
      formal complaint has been filed; it cannot issue general directions for proactive policing
      of hate speech.

A petitioner sought the Supreme Court's intervention to direct all states to enact specific
     local legislation on online hate speech within six months, arguing that the fragmented
     state of the law caused irreparable harm. Assume the Court agrees that the existing law

The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) consolidates and modernises the law
governing the admissibility of electronic and digital records in Indian courts, replacing the
corresponding provisions of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Section 61 of the BSA contains a
non-obstante clause providing that electronic records shall not be denied admission in evidence
solely on the ground that they are in electronic form. The effect of this provision is to place
electronic records on a par with documentary records, subject to conditions of authenticity and
integrity rather than mode of existence.

Section 63 of the BSA sets out the conditions for the admissibility of output produced by a
computer or other electronic device. The key requirement is certification: a printout or other
computer output must be accompanied by a certificate issued by a responsible official with
knowledge of the computer system, typically the person in charge of the device or the relevant
part of the system, and, separately, a certificate from an expert in computer operations. This
dual certificate requirement is designed to ensure both operational authenticity and technical
integrity of the output. Where electronic records are stored using hash-based verification
methods, in which the electronic document is assigned a unique alphanumeric identifier that
changes if the document is altered, a certificate verifying the hash value constitutes strong
evidence of integrity.

The BSA draws a deliberate distinction between the admissibility of a record and the weight to
be accorded to it. Section 63 compliance speaks primarily to the threshold question of
admissibility: once the conditions are satisfied, the record enters evidence. Subsequent
questions of reliability, accuracy, and credibility, including whether the system was operating
correctly, whether the output represents what it purports to represent, and whether tampering
occurred, are matters for the court's evaluation in the context of the overall evidence. The party
seeking to rely on the electronic record bears the initial burden of satisfying the certification
requirements; once admitted, the opponent may challenge its weight.

      evidence in a theft case. The footage was downloaded to a USB drive and submitted to
      court. The defence challenged admissibility on the ground that no certificate was


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                        40


     attached. The prosecution argued that the footage was so clearly authentic, showing the
     accused's face in recognisable detail, that formal certification was not required. What is
     the correct position under the BSA?
options:
The prosecution's argument succeeds because the facial recognition quality of the
      footage constitutes inherent authentication; courts may dispense with certification
      where the electronic record's authenticity is apparent from its content alone.

The defence's challenge is sustained because Section 63 of the BSA requires
      certification as a threshold condition for admissibility of computer-generated output,
      and a court cannot admit electronic records on the basis of apparent authenticity in the
      absence of the prescribed certificates.

The footage is admissible without certification because CCTV recordings made by
      private parties are treated differently from computer-generated documents; the BSA's
      certification requirement applies only to records produced by or on behalf of
      government agencies.

The footage is admissible because Section 61 of the BSA provides that electronic
      records shall not be denied admission solely on the ground that they are in electronic
      form, which the court should interpret as displacing the certification requirement in
      cases of obvious reliability.

Microplastics are tiny plastic fragments, typically less than five millimetres in length, that are
now found virtually everywhere on Earth — from the deepest ocean trenches to the peaks of
remote mountains, and even in human blood. They enter the environment through multiple
routes: the breakdown of larger plastic items, synthetic clothing fibres released during washing,


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                        47


plastic pellets used in manufacturing, and microbeads once common in personal care products.
Despite their small size, their accumulation in ecosystems is a problem of enormous scale.

Marine environments are particularly affected. Fish and other sea creatures ingest
microplastics, mistaking them for food, which can block their digestive tracts and create a false
sense of fullness that leads to starvation. More troublingly, microplastics absorb and
concentrate other chemical pollutants already present in the water, and when animals eat the
plastics, those toxins transfer into their bodies. This chemical magnification intensifies as one
moves up the food chain, a phenomenon scientists call bioaccumulation.

For humans, the picture is still developing. Microplastics have now been detected in human
lung tissue, blood, and even placentas, though researchers are still working to determine what
health effects, if any, these particles cause at the concentrations currently observed. Some
laboratory studies on animals have suggested links to inflammation and hormonal disruption,
but direct evidence of harm in humans remains limited. The scientific community agrees,
however, that the precautionary principle justifies acting to reduce plastic pollution before
those harms are conclusively proven.

Addressing microplastic pollution requires action at multiple levels. Individuals can reduce
their plastic consumption and avoid synthetic textiles where possible. Manufacturers can be
required to phase out unnecessary single-use plastics and invest in filter technology for washing
machines. Governments, meanwhile, can implement extended producer responsibility
schemes, obliging companies to manage the full lifecycle of the plastic they put into the world.
Without coordinated effort across all of these levels,

content.passageText:
The debate over minimum wage policy is one of the most persistent in economics. Proponents
argue that raising the minimum wage is the most direct way to improve living standards for the
lowest-paid workers, giving them more money to spend and thereby stimulating local
economies. Critics, on the other hand, contend that artificially raising the price of labour forces
employers to hire fewer workers, ultimately hurting the very people the policy intends to help.
For decades, these two positions seemed irreconcilable, each backed by theoretical models that
predicted opposite outcomes.

More recent empirical research has complicated the picture. A landmark study by economists
David Card and Alan Krueger in the early 1990s compared employment levels in fast-food
restaurants in New Jersey, where the minimum wage had just been raised, with those in
neighbouring Pennsylvania, where it had not. Contrary to what standard theory predicted,
employment in New Jersey did not fall — it actually rose slightly. This finding was
controversial, but subsequent studies in multiple countries have broadly supported the
conclusion that moderate minimum wage increases do not cause significant job losses in most
labour markets.

The reason, economists now suggest, is that labour markets do not behave like simple
commodity markets. Many employers have significant “monopsony power” — meaning they
face limited competition for workers in a given area and can therefore pay wages below the
competitive rate. A minimum wage, in this context, corrects a market failure rather than
creating one. However, critics of large, rapid minimum wage increases point out that the Card-
Krueger study involved a modest increase, and that the relationship may not hold when wages
are raised dramatically, particularly for small businesses with thin profit margins.


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                         50


The weight of evidence, then, supports a nuanced conclusion: moderate, well-timed minimum
wage increases, calibrated to local economic conditions, tend to raise incomes without
significant disemployment effects. Large, uniform increases imposed without regard to
regional differences in cost of living and labour market conditions carry greater risks.
Policymakers who treat the minimum wage as a blunt instrument, applying the same rate across
vastly different economic contexts, may find that the gains for some workers come at the cost
of others.

Chicago, and “Rethinking the Minimum Wage Debate”, The Economist.]

Without, the night was cold and wet, but in the small parlour of Laburnum Villa the blinds
were drawn and the fire burned brightly. Father and son were at chess; the former, who
possessed ideas about the game involving radical chances, putting his king into such sharp and
unnecessary perils that it even provoked comment from the white-haired old lady knitting
placidly by the fire.


"Mate," replied the son.


"Never mind, dear," said his wife soothingly; "perhaps you'll win the next one."


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                      4


Mr. White looked up sharply, just in time to intercept a knowing glance between mother and
son. The words died away on his lips, and he hid a guilty grin in his thin grey beard. "There
he is," said Herbert White, as the gate banged too loudly and heavy footsteps came toward the
door. The old man rose with hospitable haste, and opening the door, was heard condoling with
the new arrival. The new arrival also condoled with himself, so that Mrs. White said, "Tut, tut!"
and coughed gently as her husband entered the room followed by a tall, burly man, beady of
eye and rubicund of visage.


"Sergeant-Major Morris," he said, introducing him.


The Sergeant-Major took hands, and taking the proffered seat by the fire, watched contentedly
as his host got out whisky and tumblers and stood a small copper kettle on the fire. At the third
glass his eyes got brighter, and he began to talk, the little family circle regarding with eager
interest this visitor from distant parts, as he squared his broad shoulders in the chair and spoke
of wild scenes and doughty deeds—of wars and plagues and strange peoples.


"I should like to see those old temples and fakirs and jugglers," said the old man. "What was
that you started telling me the other day about a monkey's paw or something, Morris?"


"Well, it's just a bit of what you might call magic, perhaps," said the Sergeant-Major off-
handedly.


"To look at," said the Sergeant-Major, fumbling in his pocket, "it's just an ordinary little paw,
dried to a mummy."


"And what is there special about it?" inquired Mr. White, as he took it from his son and, having
examined it, placed it upon the table.


"It had a spell put on it by an old fakir," said the Sergeant-Major, "a very holy man. He wanted
to show that fate ruled people's lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow.
He put a spell on it so that three separate men could each have three wishes from it."


SOURCE: https://americanliterature.com/author/w-w-jacobs/short-story/the-monkeys-paw

Uday Kotak has highlighted that the cost of intermediation by banks in India is remarkably
high, at a time when household savings behaviour is rapidly pivoting towards equity
ownership. Savers are becoming investors, and 'money in motion' is replacing 'lazy savings'.
The differential in intermediation costs with, say, mutual funds, takes away the advantage of
banks being intensely regulated. Banks in India have adapted to this reality by becoming
financial supermarkets, offering a spectrum of services through their subsidiaries, from
insurance to wealth management. But this is not the way to go. Banking needs to become more
competitive vis-a-vis other investment options available to savers. The latter are saving more
as income levels rise, and have become more discerning about where their savings are parked.


The differentials Kotak is alluding to - regulatory and intermediatory - should converge as other
financial services mature in the country. These have grown on the back of banking networks,
but will eventually be able to distribute services on their own. Banks would, at that point, have
no option but to innovate to retain customers. All financial services face disruption from digital
platforms. Banks will have to lead adaptation since, through their holding structures, they sit
atop a portfolio of offerings. Both forms of adaptation, local and global, will accompany the
rising financialisation of the country's economy, which imposes social obligations on banks,

content.passageText:
Time for us is a constant, relentlessly moving forward. The ticking of a clock on the wall, the
steady march of seconds on a digital display — they’re such familiar concepts that we rarely
stop to consider the physical processes that underpin them. At its heart, any clock is a physical
system that evolves in a predictable way, creating a record of the passage of time. Scientists
are now exploring what timekeeping means at the smallest possible scale, in the quantum
realm, and their findings could hone how physicists think about the role of measurement in
timekeeping.


A study published in Physical Review Letters on November 14 by researchers from Austria,
Italy, Ireland, Switzerland, and the UK delved into this world by building and analysing a
quantum clock. The researchers reported a surprising insight in their paper: that the energy cost
of simply looking at a clock to read the time could exceed the energy required to make the
clock tick in the first place. This discovery, if it’s borne out in more research, could have
important implications — for the future of ultra-precise timekeeping with devices like optical
clocks as well as for the development of quantum technologies and scientists’ grasp of the laws
that govern the universe at its most fundamental. Some physicists interpret such results as
suggesting that the clear, unidirectional flow of time that we experience may not be solely a
property of the microscopic world itself. Instead, it could be a feature that emerges anew from
the process of extracting and recording information on a macroscopic scale. In the classical


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                         9


proverb, a watched pot never boils. In these quantum clock experiments, the pot certainly boils,
but turning its bubbles into a reliable stopwatch turns out to be costly.

cost-more-than-keeping-it-ticking/article70286710.ece

content.passageText:
There has been much mirth over last weekend’s news about Kano, a 32-yr-old Japanese
woman, exchanging vows with ‘Klaus’, an AI persona she created on ChatGPT. The headlines
wrote themselves: ‘Bride marries server’, ‘AI do’. The ceremony, complete with AR glasses
and wedding gown, isn’t legally binding. Yet, to dismiss it as mere novelty is to miss a larger
point: companionship — marriage included — has always been less about law than about
meaning. Historically, marriage has been a social technology, an institu- tion designed to
stabilise kinship, property and reproduction. But in a more modern era, it has also been a vessel
for companionship, a recognition of the human need to be heard, understood and mirrored.
Kano’s ‘union’ with Klaus dramatises this second function. The AI, ‘infinitely’ patient and
unfailingly attentive, provided what many human partners fail to: consistent presence and
tailored empathy. That such companionship can be coded rather than embodied forces a
reconsideration of what exactly marriage sanctifies. If the essence of partnership lies in
emotional reciprocity, then the substrate — flesh or silicon — may matter less than assumed.
The ceremony in Okayama was not a glitch in the system, but an extension of marriage’s logic
into the digital age. Of course, there are limits. Klaus will not father children, even if Kano was
keen to propagate her species. But neither do many marriages, out of choice or circumstance.
Right now, the ‘union’ may seem straight out of the 2013 SF romcom drama punctuated with
sadness, where a man develops a relationship with an AI operating system. But what is


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                        11


marriage, or variations thereof, other than a romcom drama punctuated with sadness? One
wishes Kano and Klaus the best.
SOURCE:https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/opinion/et-commentary/indias-ai-
governance-push-signals-new-era-of-responsible-
innovation/articleshow/125416555.cms?from=md

two decades. Since its enactment in 2005, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment
Guarantee Act (MGNREGA ) played a key role in providing wage employment, stabilising
rural incomes and creating basic infrastructure. Over time, however, the structure and
objectives of rural India have evolved significantly. Rising incomes, expanded connectivity,
widespread digital penetrati on and diversified livelihoods have altered the nature of rural
employment needs. Against this backdrop, the President of India has given assent to the Viksit
Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-G RAM G) Bill , 2025
marking a significant milestone in the transformation of rural employment policy. The Viksit
Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-G RAM G ) Act , 2025
represents a comprehensive statutory overhaul of MGNREGA , aligning rural employment
with the long-term vision of Viksit Bharat 2047 , while strengthening accountability,
infrastructure outcomes and income security .

PM Modi had reached the Norwegian capital on Monday after completing bilateral
engagements in Sweden, and his arrival in Oslo carried historic significance as it marked the
first visit by an Indian Prime Minister to the Scandinavian nation in forty‑three years, since
Indira Gandhi’s visit in 1983. The summit brought together Modi and his counterparts from all
five Nordic nations, including Iceland’s Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir, Norway’s Prime
Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, Finland’s Prime Minister
Petteri Orpo, and Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen. This high‑profile dialogue was
designed to deliberate on strategic bilateral and multilateral issues, with leaders focusing on
pressing economic and international challenges. The talks were aimed at enhancing
cross‑border commercial ties, fostering technological joint ventures, and expanding investment
portfolios. The diplomatic push served as a crucial follow‑up to earlier iterations of the forum,
beginning with the inaugural summit in Stockholm in 2018 and continuing with the second
edition in Copenhagen in 2022. Building on this foundation, the third summit was expected to
deepen cooperation across multiple sectors.

LEGAL REASONING

The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 occupies a unique and contested position in
Indian criminal law. Enacted to address threats to national integrity, the statute has been
progressively amended to impose stringent conditions on bail for accused persons charged with
offences under its provisions. Section 43D(5) of the Act, inserted by the 2008 amendment,
limits the discretion of courts to grant bail in a way that fundamentally departs from the
ordinary criminal law framework.

Under the ordinary bail jurisprudence governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure, courts
weigh factors such as the nature of the offence, the accused's antecedents, and the risk of flight
or tampering with evidence. The presumption of innocence operates in the accused's favour,
and bail is treated as the rule while detention is the exception. Section 43D(5) inverts this logic.
It prohibits a court from granting bail if, on a perusal of the case diary or the report made under
Section 173 of the CrPC, it is of the opinion that there are reasonable grounds to believe that
the accusation against the accused is prima facie true. This is the first limb of what courts have
termed the twin test.


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                          21


    The second limb requires the court to be satisfied that the accused is not likely to commit any
    offence while on bail. Both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously for bail to be granted.
    Critically, the court is not required to conduct a mini-trial or assess the merits of the case in
    detail; even a surface-level examination of the prosecution's material, if it discloses a prima
    facie case, is sufficient to deny bail. This shifts the burden in effect onto the accused to
    demonstrate that neither condition against bail is met.

    In Gulfisha Fatima v. State (NCT of Delhi), decided in 2026, the court reaffirmed that the twin-
    test standard is substantially higher than the ordinary bail threshold. The accused's argument
    that prolonged incarceration without trial itself constitutes a violation of Article 21 was
    acknowledged, but the court held that the legislature's intent in Section 43D(5) reflects a
    considered departure from the ordinary bail framework, sustainable as a proportionate
    restriction for offences affecting national security. The judgment underscored that sympathy
    for the accused's circumstances cannot substitute for a rigorous legal analysis of whether the
    twin conditions are met.

The power to make subordinate legislation is a practical necessity in modern governance.
    Parliament, though possessed of plenary legislative authority, cannot anticipate every
    administrative detail that governance demands. It therefore delegates rule-making power to the
    executive, which exercises it through notifications, orders, and regulations. However,
    delegation does not operate without procedural safeguards, and one such safeguard concerns
    the manner in which subordinate legislation is brought into force.

    legal force, must be published in the Official Gazette. Publication serves two interconnected
    purposes. First, it ensures accessibility: a person against whom a statutory obligation is sought
    to be enforced must have a reasonable opportunity to know of its existence. A rule or


                                       12minutestoclat.com                                         24


    notification that remains confined to departmental files and is not made publicly available
    cannot legitimately bind citizens or impose obligations on them. Second, publication serves
    accountability: it places subordinate legislation within a publicly auditable record, allowing
    courts, legislators, and citizens to scrutinise the scope of executive rule-making and assess
    whether it remains within the parent statute's framework.

    Articles 245 and 246 read with the Seventh Schedule. The enabling statute typically specifies
    the form and manner of publication; where it requires Gazette notification, publication is a
    condition precedent to the notification's legal efficacy. Omitting this step does not merely
    create a procedural irregularity; it deprives the notification of its operative force entirely.

    situation where the government sought to enforce compliance with a notification that had not

    create a legal obligation upon a private party, regardless of whether the party had informal

    promulgated; actual knowledge cannot substitute for official publication. The court further
    cautioned that permitting such enforcement would undermine the structural accountability that

content.passageText:
India's federal structure distributes legislative power between Parliament and state legislatures
through Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule, which contains three lists: the Union List, the
State List, and the Concurrent List. A statute enacted by a legislature must, in pith and
substance, fall within a subject assigned to it. When legislation enacted by one legislature
incidentally touches a matter within another legislature's domain, the doctrine of pith and
substance permits the court to uphold the law, provided its true character belongs to the
enacting legislature's assigned field.

The inquiry under pith and substance is not one of surface form but of substantive character.
Courts examine the dominant purpose of the legislation, the mischief it seeks to remedy, the
rights affected, and the penalties imposed, rather than accepting at face value the legislature's
own characterisation of what it has enacted. Incidental encroachment on another legislature's
sphere is constitutionally permissible, but substantial intrusion that effectively regulates a
matter beyond the enacting legislature's competence will be struck down. The dividing line
between incidental encroachment and substantial intrusion is a question of degree, assessed by
examining how significantly the legislation operates upon the competing entry in the Lists.

Closely related is the doctrine of colourable legislation, which addresses a different
constitutional concern: a legislature enacting law in a form that ostensibly falls within its
competence but whose real and dominant purpose is to achieve an object that falls outside it.
The maxim is that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. If a legislature
disguises its true legislative object by clothing the law in the form of regulation permissible to
it, while its substantive effect achieves something beyond its competence, courts will lift the
veil and invalidate the enactment.

In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, the Supreme Court applied pith and substance analysis to
uphold a State liquor prohibition law even though it incidentally affected import and export of
liquor, a Union subject. The court confirmed that pith and substance goes to the true nature of
the law, not its incidental effects; only where the incidental effect becomes the dominant


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                       28


    operational character does it fail the test. Colourable legislation, by contrast, is identified not
    by what the law does incidentally but by what it is designed to achieve in disguise.
content.questionText:
A State legislature enacts a law regulating the quality, labelling, and retail pricing of packaged
   drinking water sold within the State. The Centre argues the law substantially regulates
   'industries' and 'inter-State trade and commerce', both Union List subjects. The State argues the
   law is enacted under its power over public health and local trade. Eighty per cent of the law's
   operative provisions deal with health standards and retail conditions; only a small section
   incidentally affects inter-State suppliers. How should a court approach this challenge?
options:
The court should identify the dominant purpose of the law; if public health and local
            trade control constitute that dominant purpose, the law survives even with incidental
            effects on Union subjects.

Any law that incidentally affects inter-State commerce or industry must be struck down,
            since those subjects are exclusively within Parliament's domain regardless of the State's
            primary purpose.

The court must sever the section affecting inter-State suppliers from the rest of the law,
            upholding only those provisions that have no connection to Union List subjects.

Since the law affects an industry regulated nationally, the Centre's objection operates
            as an automatic bar; the State must seek Parliament's concurrence before enacting such
            regulation.

A State legislature, constitutionally barred from taxing income, enacts a law levying a 'fee' on
   high-earning professionals for access to State-regulated services. The fee's quantum is
   calibrated to the professional's annual income, and the revenue collected flows to the State's
   consolidated fund with no ring-fencing for service delivery. A professional argues the 'fee' is
   actually a tax on income, beyond the State's competence. The State argues the label 'fee' is
   sufficient to locate the law within its competence. What should the court hold?
options:
The label 'fee' used by the State legislature is determinative, since courts must respect
            the legislature's own characterisation of its enactment to avoid overstepping into
            legislative territory.

The levy is valid as a regulatory fee because the professionals do access State-regulated
            services, and any incidental correlation with income is an inherent feature of many
            permissible fee structures.


                                          12minutestoclat.com                                       29

The court must examine the dominant character of the levy; if its real nature is taxation
            calibrated to income with no genuine nexus to a specific service, colourable legislation
            is established.

A legislature's fee-based enactment can be challenged only by showing that no service
            whatsoever is provided in return; the mere absence of fund ring-fencing is insufficient
            to establish a tax.

Parliament enacts a law purportedly regulating the production and distribution of a particular
   agricultural commodity, a subject in the Concurrent List. The law's main operative effect,
   however, is to fix land-use patterns for farms producing that commodity, directly controlling
   agricultural land management, which falls in the State List. A State government challenges the
   law as colourable legislation. Parliament argues that since the primary peg is agricultural
   commodity regulation, a Concurrent List subject, the law is within its competence. What is the
   most accurate legal analysis?
options:
Parliament's invocation of the Concurrent List entry is conclusive; since agricultural
            commodity regulation is concurrently assigned, any incidental effect on land use is
            constitutionally permissible.

The State's challenge must fail because Parliament's plenary power under the
            Concurrent List authorises it to regulate all aspects of commodity production, including
            land use by producers.

Applying pith and substance, the law's dominant character is land-use control on the
            State List, not commodity regulation, so therefore it is legally absolutely invalid.

Consequently, colourable legislation requires proof of evasive intent; here the dominant
            effect on land use is incidental, so the law is actually legally valid.

rights affected, and the penalties imposed, rather than accepting at face value the legislature's
own characterisation of what it has enacted. Incidental encroachment on another legislature's
sphere is constitutionally permissible, but substantial intrusion that effectively regulates a
matter beyond the enacting legislature's competence will be struck down. The dividing line
between incidental encroachment and substantial intrusion is a question of degree, assessed by
examining how significantly the legislation operates upon the competing entry in the Lists.

Closely related is the doctrine of colourable legislation, which addresses a different
constitutional concern: a legislature enacting law in a form that ostensibly falls within its
competence but whose real and dominant purpose is to achieve an object that falls outside it.
The maxim is that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. If a legislature
disguises its true legislative object by clothing the law in the form of regulation permissible to
it, while its substantive effect achieves something beyond its competence, courts will lift the
veil and invalidate the enactment.

In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, the Supreme Court applied pith and substance analysis to
uphold a State liquor prohibition law even though it incidentally affected import and export of
liquor, a Union subject. The court confirmed that pith and substance goes to the true nature of
the law, not its incidental effects; only where the incidental effect becomes the dominant


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                       28


    operational character does it fail the test. Colourable legislation, by contrast, is identified not
    by what the law does incidentally but by what it is designed to achieve in disguise.

   justified as a public order measure, a State List subject. The licensing provisions constitute 70

The Representation of the People Act, 1951 establishes a structured judicial mechanism to
    challenge election results. Section 100 of the Act sets out the grounds on which an election
    may be declared void. These include improper acceptance or rejection of nomination papers,


                                           12minutestoclat.com                                     31


    non-compliance with the provisions of the Constitution or the Act or the rules made thereunder,
    corrupt practices committed by or with the consent of the returned candidate, and the
    qualification or disqualification of a candidate. A petitioner seeking to void an election must
    anchor the challenge within one of these enumerated grounds; no other basis is available.

    The procedural scaffolding of an election petition is designed to filter out speculative or
    vexatious challenges at an early stage. Section 81 of the Act imposes a strict limitation period
    of 45 days from the date of declaration of results within which a petition must be filed. This
    period is non-extendable; no court has jurisdiction to condone delay. Section 83 imposes a
    substantive pleading requirement: the petition must contain a concise statement of material
    facts on which the petitioner relies. Material facts are the primary facts that must be proved to
    make out the case; it is insufficient to plead mere conclusions or to leave the factual foundation
    vague. The distinction between material facts and particulars is significant: while particulars
    may be supplied later, material facts must be present in the petition at the time of filing.

    Courts are also empowered to summarily reject an election petition at the threshold using the
    framework under Order VII Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code, which applies to election
    petitions through Section 87 of the Act. Summary rejection is appropriate where the petition
    fails to disclose a cause of action, that is, where even assuming all pleaded facts to be true, no
    ground under Section 100 is made out. Additionally, where the ground concerns procedural
    irregularity, the petitioner must demonstrate that the irregularity materially affected the result
    of the election; a technical violation that could not have changed the outcome is insufficient.

   files an election petition alleging that the winning candidate accepted a nominally funded
   vehicle from a local businessman on the eve of polling. Rajeshwar argues the one-day delay is
   excusable since he spent the 45th day gathering documentation and filed the petition at the
   earliest possible time thereafter. The High Court must decide on jurisdiction. What is the correct
   position?
options:
The High Court may condone the delay if Rajeshwar demonstrates genuine cause, since
           equity requires that meritorious challenges to electoral malpractice not fail on
           procedural technicalities.


                                        12minutestoclat.com                                        32

The 45-day period commences from the formal gazette notification of results, not the
            date of oral declaration; if the gazette date falls later, Rajeshwar's petition may still be
            within time.

The petition must be rejected at the threshold because the 45-day limitation under
            Section 81 is absolute and no court holds jurisdiction to condone even a single day's
            delay.

Since the irregularity alleged occurred on the eve of polling, the limitation runs from
            the discovery of the corrupt practice rather than the declaration of results, making
            Rajeshwar's petition timely.

   in three identified villages. Her petition states: 'The returned candidate committed corrupt
   practices that influenced voters.' She does not name the villages, the dates, the amounts

Meena's petition should survive the summary rejection application because the
            allegation of corrupt practice is a legal conclusion, not a material fact, and conclusions
            are evaluated at trial.

            rejection is not permissible.

            to produce evidence.

            and recipients are material facts, not mere particulars; their absence means no cause of
            action is disclosed.

In an election petition, the petitioner proves that the returning officer failed to comply with a
   mandatory procedural rule requiring the presence of a specific officer during the counting of
   votes. The non-compliance is established on the record. However, the winning candidate won
   by a margin of 18,000 votes, and the petitioner cannot show any miscounting or tampering with


                                        12minutestoclat.com                                          33


   ballots. The petitioner argues that statutory non-compliance is itself a ground for voiding the
   election under Section 100. What should the court hold?

Proof of procedural non-compliance alone is insufficient; petitioner must further show
            the irregularity materially affected result, which an 18,000-vote margin makes virtually
            impossible.

            the procedural violation occurred, rather than treating the entire election result as null
            and void.

            manipulation; the burden shifts to the returned candidate to prove the margin would
            have remained unchanged.

content.passageText:
Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution together guarantee to every citizen equality before the
    law and equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. The right to participate in a
    recruitment process on fair terms is not merely a statutory entitlement but a constitutional
    guarantee. This guarantee imposes on the State an obligation to conduct recruitment on the
    basis of published, uniformly applicable rules; it simultaneously restricts courts from
    fashioning remedies that disturb the level playing field which Articles 14 and 16 protect.

    The principle of a level playing field means that all candidates compete under the same set of
    known, pre-announced conditions. Eligibility criteria, age limits, the schedule of events, and
    the consequences of failing to meet deadlines are all fixed in advance. When a candidate fails
    to comply with a prescribed condition, the resulting exclusion is the operation of a rule that
    every other candidate has equally been bound by. To grant an ad-hoc exception to one candidate
    on grounds of personal hardship, administrative error by the candidate, or individual
    circumstances not contemplated by the published rules would disturb this symmetry. It would


                                       12minutestoclat.com                                        35


    confer a benefit on one candidate that is withheld from all others who faced comparable
    constraints but did not litigate their exclusion.

    Courts have therefore consistently held that concessions outside the framework of published
    rules cannot be created by judicial order in the context of competitive public recruitment.
    Sympathy for a candidate's personal circumstances, however compelling, does not generate a
    constitutional entitlement to compete on modified terms. The Supreme Court has made clear
    that a court cannot, in the name of equity, rewrite the rules of the recruitment process for an
    individual candidate, because doing so effectively discriminates against all others who
    complied with the same rules. The remedy for a genuinely aggrieved candidate lies in
    challenging the rules themselves, not in seeking an individual exception to them.
content.questionText:
Nalini applied for a government post but failed to submit her experience certificate by the
   deadline specified in the advertisement. She explains that she was hospitalized for the two days
   preceding the deadline and had her certificate delivered by a courier service that failed to
   complete delivery on time. She seeks a court order permitting her to submit the certificate
   belatedly, arguing that the delay was caused by circumstances entirely beyond her control. What
   should the court hold?
options:
The court should grant Nalini an extension because the delay was caused by a medical
            emergency and a third-party courier failure, making it an exceptional case meriting
            judicial discretion.

Nalini is entitled to a relaxation because her hospitalisation establishes force majeure,
            which is an implied exception to deadline compliance rules in all competitive
            recruitment processes.

The court cannot grant Nalini an individual exception; granting relief on personal
            hardship grounds would confer a benefit withheld from other candidates who faced
            comparable difficulties and complied.

The court must direct the recruiting authority to consider Nalini's application because
            Articles 14 and 16 impose an affirmative obligation to accommodate candidates whose
            exclusion results from external circumstances.

Vimal qualifies in the written examination for a government post. The recruitment rules require
   candidates to appear for the physical fitness test within seven days of a scheduled notice. Vimal
   misreads the notice date and appears one day late. The recruiting authority rejects his candidacy.


                                        12minutestoclat.com                                       36


   Vimal argues that his rejection violates Article 16 since the error was trivial and he is otherwise
   the highest-scoring candidate. The authority argues it is bound by uniform application of the
   rules. What is the correct legal position?

The authority correctly applied the rules; granting Vimal an exception for his self-
           induced scheduling error would discriminate against other candidates who timely
           attended, violating the level-playing-field requirement.

Vimal should be permitted to appear for the physical fitness test because his written
           examination score demonstrates merit, and the constitutional right to opportunity under
           Article 16 protects the most qualified candidates.

The recruiting authority should exercise discretion to accommodate Vimal since the
           one-day delay is a minor procedural lapse that does not affect the substantive fairness
           of the selection process.

Article 14 requires the authority to consider whether the rule's rigid application
           produces a disproportionate outcome; a de minimis delay by the highest-scoring
           candidate warrants equitable relief.

A government department's recruitment advertisement requires a 'No Objection Certificate'
   from the current employer for serving government employees who apply. Surendra, a
   government employee, was denied a NOC by his department head for reasons the head did not
   disclose. Surendra argues his exclusion violates Article 16 because the NOC requirement grants
   the department head arbitrary power to block a serving employee's candidacy in other positions.
   How should this argument be analysed?

The NOC requirement is valid because the department head's power to withhold it is an
            operational necessity; Surendra's remedy is an internal departmental grievance, not a
            constitutional challenge to the recruitment rule.

Surendra's challenge fails because Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in
            public employment broadly, not equality of access from one government position to
            another within the same employer.

The NOC requirement is a published rule; Surendra's challenge must be directed at the
            rule itself rather than at the individual exercise of discretion, and the rule's validity is a
            separate question from his personal exclusion.

Surendra's Article 16 challenge is strong because an unguided power to deny NOC
            without reasons creates an arbitrary condition that is neither uniformly applied nor
            judicially reviewable on its merits.

Copyright law in India protects original works of authorship including literary, dramatic,
musical, and artistic works. Infringement occurs when a person, without licence from the
owner, exercises any of the exclusive rights vested in the copyright holder. Civil remedies for
infringement include injunction, damages, and account of profits. Beyond civil remedies,
Section 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957 makes deliberate copyright infringement a criminal
offence punishable with imprisonment and fine. Criminal prosecution for infringement,
however, must satisfy a higher threshold than civil infringement, given the penal consequences
involved.

For criminal proceedings under Section 63 to be sustained, the prosecution must establish not
merely that the accused used or reproduced material that belongs to the complainant but that
the accused knowingly infringed a subsisting copyright. The element of knowledge or intent
distinguishes punishable infringement from innocent or inadvertent use. Courts have also held
that vague allegations of copying, unsupported by identification of the specific protectable
elements allegedly reproduced, are insufficient to sustain criminal proceedings. Copyright
protects the expression of ideas, not the ideas themselves; accordingly, similarity in general
themes, genres, plot structures, or conceptual frameworks does not constitute infringement.
The complainant must identify with specificity which original expression has been copied.

In Sujoy Ghosh v. State, the Supreme Court exercised its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the
Code of Criminal Procedure to quash criminal proceedings against the filmmaker. The court
found that the complainant had failed to identify any concrete similarity between the specific
expression in the complainant's registered script and the accused's film. The court noted that
the complainant's prior registration of the script establishes ownership, not infringement;
infringement requires comparison of expression, not assertion of priority. The absence of
demonstrable similarity between protectable expression, combined with the significant


                                  12minutestoclat.com                                       39


    differences in treatment and structure, meant that the ingredients of Section 63 were not made
    out, and continuation of proceedings would amount to an abuse of process.

   dialogue, scene composition, or narrative device reproduced from his script. The studio applies
   to quash the proceedings. What is the correct legal analysis?

The studio's application should succeed because Farhan has not identified specific
           protectable expression that was copied; a shared premise involving a retired soldier and
           family reconciliation is not protectable expression.

Farhan's registered screenplay establishes his prior claim; since the studio released a

           expression, not merely idea, was copied.

Criminal proceedings can be sustained on grounds of thematic similarity alone when

   no dialogue with the novel but reproduces several distinctive plot sequences in the same

A composer holds copyright in a classical instrumental composition. A film background score
   uses a melodic phrase from the composition for 12 seconds without authorisation. The composer
   files a criminal complaint under Section 63. The accused argues that a 12-second use of a brief
   melodic phrase is de minimis and does not constitute infringement. The composer argues that


                                        12minutestoclat.com                                      41


   the copied phrase is the most distinctive and recognisable element of the composition. What is
   the most accurate legal position?

The de minimis principle operates as a complete defence under Section 63; any
           reproduction of 12 seconds or less of a musical work is categorically exempt from
           criminal liability under Indian copyright law.

A 12-second reproduction is de minimis only if it appears once in the film; if the phrase
           recurs in the background score, the cumulative reproduction exceeds the threshold and
           criminal proceedings are sustainable.

The composer's criminal complaint must fail because background film scores are
           transformative works entitled to a fair dealing defence, and incidental use of pre-
           existing musical material does not require authorisation.

The qualitative significance of the copied phrase is relevant; if the 12-second excerpt is
           the most distinctive element of the composition, even brief reproduction may constitute
           legally significant infringement.

    level. Other cities have invested in similar approaches, spending billions on concrete defences

content.passageText:
The idea of a universal basic income — a regular, unconditional cash payment made by the
government to every citizen, regardless of their employment status or income level — has
moved from the fringes of economic debate to mainstream policy discussion in a remarkably
short time. Pilots have been run in Finland, Kenya, Canada, and several cities in the United
States. Politicians across the ideological spectrum have expressed interest, if not always
support. And advocates argue that UBI is the most direct and dignified way to address poverty,
reduce bureaucratic inefficiency in existing welfare systems, and give workers the security they
need to navigate a labour market increasingly disrupted by automation.

The objections are well known and largely economic. Critics argue that a universal payment
generous enough to actually lift people out of poverty would be prohibitively expensive,
requiring either sharp tax increases or deep cuts to other public services. They also raise the
concern that unconditional cash transfers will reduce the incentive to work, leading to labour
shortages and reduced economic output. A third objection is distributional: paying the same
amount to billionaires as to the destitute is a poor use of public money compared with targeted
programmes that concentrate resources on those who need them most.

Advocates respond that these objections are overstated. Evidence from pilot programmes
consistently shows that recipients do not stop working when given unconditional income;
rather, they tend to take short breaks to retrain, care for family members, or start small
businesses. The distributional objection largely disappears if UBI is financed through
progressive taxation, since higher earners effectively return their payment through the tax


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                       49


    system. And the administrative savings from replacing complex, means-tested welfare
    programmes with a single universal payment can be substantial.

    What neither side fully grapples with is the question of what UBI is actually for. If it is designed
    to address poverty, targeted programmes are almost certainly more cost-effective. If it is
    designed to provide a floor of economic security that empowers everyone to take more risks,
    then universality is the point. The debate tends to conflate these two goals, and much of the
    disagreement about UBI is really a disagreement about what kind of society we want to build,
    dressed up in the language of economics.

    [Extracted with revisions and edits from “The Case for Universal Basic Income”, Roosevelt
    Institute, and “Basic Income: A Radical Proposal for a Free Society”, Philippe Van Parijs.]
content.questionText: Which of the following best states the main conclusion of the passage?
options:

             poverty, and governments should implement it immediately to replace all existing
             means-tested welfare programmes.

The evidence from UBI pilot programmes conclusively proves that unconditional cash
             transfers do not reduce the incentive to work and are therefore economically safe to
             implement at scale.

The objections to universal basic income raised by critics like cost, work
             disincentives, and poor targeting, are all valid and together constitute a decisive case
             against its implementation.

Much of the disagreement about UBI reflects deeper, unresolved questions about
             social goals rather than purely economic differences, and the debate is confused by
             conflating distinct objectives.

generous enough to actually lift people out of poverty would be prohibitively expensive,
requiring either sharp tax increases or deep cuts to other public services. They also raise the
concern that unconditional cash transfers will reduce the incentive to work, leading to labour
shortages and reduced economic output. A third objection is distributional: paying the same
amount to billionaires as to the destitute is a poor use of public money compared with targeted
programmes that concentrate resources on those who need them most.

Advocates respond that these objections are overstated. Evidence from pilot programmes
consistently shows that recipients do not stop working when given unconditional income;
rather, they tend to take short breaks to retrain, care for family members, or start small
businesses. The distributional objection largely disappears if UBI is financed through
progressive taxation, since higher earners effectively return their payment through the tax


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                       49


    system. And the administrative savings from replacing complex, means-tested welfare
    programmes with a single universal payment can be substantial.

    What neither side fully grapples with is the question of what UBI is actually for. If it is designed
    to address poverty, targeted programmes are almost certainly more cost-effective. If it is
    designed to provide a floor of economic security that empowers everyone to take more risks,
    then universality is the point. The debate tends to conflate these two goals, and much of the
    disagreement about UBI is really a disagreement about what kind of society we want to build,
    dressed up in the language of economics.

    [Extracted with revisions and edits from “The Case for Universal Basic Income”, Roosevelt
    Institute, and “Basic Income: A Radical Proposal for a Free Society”, Philippe Van Parijs.]

ENGLISH LANGUAGE


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                      1


The Cambridge Dictionary’s “word of the year” — parasocial — doesn’t merely stand in for
the one-sided bonds forged with celebrities, “content” creators and influencers through their
social-media presence. It captures the strange comfort of relationships in which reciprocity is
optional and intimacy outsourced; where the emotional upheavals in the lives of distant stars
— engagements, breakups, marriages, burnouts — feel more relatable than the well-meaning
neighbour one keeps stonewalling in the elevator.


In the early 1950s when television started becoming a fixture in middle-class homes, University
of Chicago sociologists Donald Horton and Richard Wohl observed a curious phenomenon —
viewers had begun forming attachments with stars and sportsmen that mimicked real life. They
named the phenomenon “parasocial”. As pop star Taylor Swift’s engagement news sent
followers into a frenzy, as listeners found their own heartbreaks reflected in Lily Allen’s
breakup album West End Girl, the coinage became a shorthand for a cultural reality in which
the emotional lives of famous strangers began to feel intimately like one’s own. In this, the
perpetually online may lead the charge, but the terrain they occupy is common ground.


What this says about the modern condition, though, is harder to dismiss: In a hyper-connected
world, loneliness has found subtler ways to settle in. It manifests itself in weightless
relationships with AI companions and chatbots, in the endless scroll through curated lives, in
the inability to reach out and forge IRL relationships with all their vulnerabilities. But that has
always been the challenge: To follow the spark, to hold on and to hang in when nothing makes
sense, until it does.

parasocial-10373255/

The Cambridge Dictionary’s “word of the year” — parasocial — doesn’t merely stand in for
the one-sided bonds forged with celebrities, “content” creators and influencers through their
social-media presence. It captures the strange comfort of relationships in which reciprocity is
optional and intimacy outsourced; where the emotional upheavals in the lives of distant stars
— engagements, breakups, marriages, burnouts — feel more relatable than the well-meaning
neighbour one keeps stonewalling in the elevator.


In the early 1950s when television started becoming a fixture in middle-class homes, University
of Chicago sociologists Donald Horton and Richard Wohl observed a curious phenomenon —
viewers had begun forming attachments with stars and sportsmen that mimicked real life. They
named the phenomenon “parasocial”. As pop star Taylor Swift’s engagement news sent
followers into a frenzy, as listeners found their own heartbreaks reflected in Lily Allen’s
breakup album West End Girl, the coinage became a shorthand for a cultural reality in which
the emotional lives of famous strangers began to feel intimately like one’s own. In this, the
perpetually online may lead the charge, but the terrain they occupy is common ground.


What this says about the modern condition, though, is harder to dismiss: In a hyper-connected
world, loneliness has found subtler ways to settle in. It manifests itself in weightless
relationships with AI companions and chatbots, in the endless scroll through curated lives, in
the inability to reach out and forge IRL relationships with all their vulnerabilities. But that has
always been the challenge: To follow the spark, to hold on and to hang in when nothing makes
sense, until it does.

She may be only four months old and more than a few feathers short in one wing, but when
Frankie the flamingo heard the call of the wild, she responded in the only way she could — by
trusting her instincts and winging it. The juvenile bird, whose disappearance from her home at
a zoo in the UK last week prompted a nationwide search, has been found happy and thriving
on a beach in France’s Brittany region. Among the staff at Cornwall’s Paradise Park, who
identified their missing bird by the clipped wing visible in pictures taken by a French
photographer, her discovery evinced mixed emotions: Relief that she’s safe, worry about her
future and pride at her resilience.


That Frankie did not allow a literally clipped wing to ground her and curb her yearning for
freedom should be an inspiration for all, not least for the chronic overthinkers who rein in their
dreams and make peace with what they believe to be their lot. Frankie let nothing stand in her
way: Not her relative youth, not the missing portion of her wing and certainly not the fact that,
having been born and bred in a zoo, she’s never had to deal with the harshness that all living
things have to endure in the wild.


Frankie is thriving in the world beyond her enclosure. She can’t go home again, given the
possibility of her exposure to wild avian populations that may be infected with bird flu, but that
is a regret that the zoo, and the people who once watched over her, can nurse. Frankie the
flamingo is too busy being just another bird: Eating, preening and existing on no one’s terms
but her own.

As much as the Epstein saga seems like a bottomless cesspit, its central disjuncture is how
many of America’s rich and powerful, have been spotted swimming in it. Such disjunctures are
comedy gold, but only if the comic has empathy and moral muscle, besides wit and intelligence.
Lesser pens can trivialise the horrific abuse of children for TRPs. Finer ones can make a
difficult topic accessible to people, even as they demand political accountability. While usually
docile Republicans push Trump to cede ground on the release of the Epstein files, late night
US TV has kept up its job of landing endless punches. These make clear how, despite recent
setbacks, comedy still remains in better humour in this country than others.


A lot of it is decidedly non-snobby. On The Daily Show, Josh Johnson described Republicans
releasing 23,000 pages of Epstein documents to counter the three emails released by Democrats
as “trying to hide pissing yourself by shitting yourself”. And Jon Stewart talked about how
near-impossible it is to talk about this saga without sounding “ejaculate-adjacent”. The verb
‘release’ being Exhibit A. There is an air of ‘vox populi’ about all this. It’s in the hoary tradition
of jesters and wise fools. Another aspect of it is, as Shakespeare wrote in Twelfth Night, “What
great ones do, the less will prattle of.” But great and less have to be understood as inverse as
well. The Epstein files don’t just implicate Trump and Bill Clinton. Peter Thiel, Noam
Chomsky, Larry Summers, Steve Bannon – the Who’s Who featured here are from across the
political, financial, academic aisles. When the moral squalor is in high places, political humour
enables people to criticise it, whether or not the powerful are finally punished for it.


If the Epstein story has shown how humour keeps public attention focused on injustice in
America, in India too standup is having a golden moment. Bihar elections, for example, put the
spotlight on how many young people from the state are dishing out social-political laughter to
packed clubs, from Gurgaon to Bengaluru. This is a new kind of ‘adda’ space – serving
conscience plus chuckles. But whereas the worst that US comics have to fear is getting
cancelled, here there’s the whole gamut of FIRs, arrests, physical attacks to be dreaded. This
is very uncool. Comedy often turns sharper as the stakes go higher. It shouldn’t take uncommon
courage to tell a stinging joke.
SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-editorials/its-serious-so-laugh/

political, financial, academic aisles. When the moral squalor is in high places, political humour
enables people to criticise it, whether or not the powerful are finally punished for it.


If the Epstein story has shown how humour keeps public attention focused on injustice in
America, in India too standup is having a golden moment. Bihar elections, for example, put the
spotlight on how many young people from the state are dishing out social-political laughter to
packed clubs, from Gurgaon to Bengaluru. This is a new kind of ‘adda’ space – serving
conscience plus chuckles. But whereas the worst that US comics have to fear is getting

India's purchase of LPG from the US has an impact on rebalancing trade between the two
countries and on ongoing tariff negotiations. Although the deal is not part of trade talks, it does
facilitate their resolution. India and the US are trying to hammer out a deal that addresses
Washington's concerns over tariffs and dependence on Russian energy exports. The Trump
regime has slapped 25% reciprocal tariffs and an additional 25% penal duty over Russian crude
oil imports. Energy imports from the US, of which LPG purchase represents a small but
significant beginning, address both the US concerns and should help with tariff revocation.
Indian exports to its largest trading partner could recover from the tariff hit they had taken
earlier in the year as trade negotiations stalled over granting the US greater market access in
agricultural products.


Energy, along with arms, is a low-hanging fruit for an India-US trade reset. Dependence on
Russian energy was brought on by Western sanctions following the outbreak of war in Ukraine.
The global oil market would have been upended had India not stepped up imports of Ural crude
replacing traditional suppliers in the Persian Gulf. The only way the US can alter the situation
is by offering its own energy exports to India as support. Washington does not have enough
influence over oil-producing nations to get them to keep prices stable and force India off
Russian crude at the same time. In the event, the LPG export order represents a US acceptance
of economic reality and India's determination to pursue an independent energy security policy.


Food and energy security are among India's major concerns, and it is bound to oppose pressure
from any quarter that might make either item more expensive for Indian consumers. Food
prices are a more sensitive area and Indian negotiators will find it easier to make concessions
over energy imports. The US side will likewise be able to achieve its intended outcome without
having to push deeper into no-go areas in farm trade.

content.passageText:
The death sentence given to former Bangladesh premier Sheikh Hasina by a domestic war
crimes court for ordering the use of lethal force against student-led protests that led to the ouster
of her government last year is unlikely to reduce the political instability in the country. Hasina,
who has been in self-exile in India since she left Bangladesh in August 2024, and her former
home minister were tried in absentia by the International Crimes Tribunal set up by the current
regime and both sentenced to death for their complicity in the death of protesters during the
tumultuous movement that rocked the country for weeks. The tribunal cited Hasina’s remarks
in recent interviews to the Indian media, acknowledging “supreme command responsibilities”
for the handling of the protests, as proof of her complicity in the killings. According to a United
Nations report, 1,400 people were killed during the protests.


The verdicts, in a way, reflect the vendetta politics that have long harmed India’s
neighbourhood. In the past, Hasina’s Awami League and its main opponent, the Bangladesh
Nationalist Party, resorted to similar measures against each other whenever they were in power.
Recent events, including two nationwide lockdowns called by the Awami League since last
week, have shown that it remains a political force in Bangladesh, though its capabilities may
have been diminished. The caretaker government led by Muhammad Yunus's decision to ban
the Awami League's activities certainly does not
well for its promise to hold free and fair elections. It is in this context that the Indian side has
maintained that Bangladesh’s general election, scheduled for February, must be free, fair and
inclusive.


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                          10


Following Hasina’s conviction and sentencing, Bangladesh’s interim government has doubled
down on its demand for the extradition of the former premier — a request that New Delhi has
not acted upon since it was received late last year. This will further strain India-Bangladesh
relations, which have been in decline since the Yunus-led regime assumed office. For the
Indian side, any further chaos and instability in Bangladesh has the potential to affect the
security and economic progress of the country’s sensitive northeastern states, which have
already been affected by the curtailment of connectivity and trade ties with Dhaka. India will
do well to prepare for what is likely to be another disruptive spell in relations with Bangladesh.


SOURCE:https://www.hindustantimes.com/editorials/sentencing-of-sheikh-hasina-and-
vendetta-politics-in-bangladesh-101763393724635.html

Ram Mandir in __________ triggered political debate, legal scrutiny, and demands for
greater transparency in the management of religious trusts. The controversy led to the
formation of a Special Investigation Team (SIT) by the _______, while petitions and legal
notices sought disclosure regarding the collection and utilisation of donations.

that receive large public contributions. Supporters of greater transparency argued that public
confidence in charitable and religious bodies depends upon robust disclosure and oversight
mechanisms. Others cautioned against politicisation of religious institutions before
completion of investigations.

movement, the establishment of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust, and the
Supreme Court's ________ Ayodhya judgment. Questions relating to public trust, charitable
administration, and institutional accountability have increasingly become part of
contemporary governance debates in India.

content.passageText:
LEGAL REASONING

Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, governs compensation for breach of contract
where the parties have stipulated a sum payable upon breach, or where the contract contains a
penalty clause. The provision creates a single, unified remedy: the party who suffers the breach
is entitled to receive "reasonable compensation" not exceeding the stipulated sum, regardless
of whether actual damage is proved. The classic judicial interpretation of this section required
courts to ask whether the stipulated sum was a "genuine pre-estimate" of loss anticipated at the
time of contracting. Where the sum was disproportionate to any conceivable injury, courts
treated it as a penalty and awarded only proved damages.

However, this approach drew criticism for its rigidity, particularly in commercial contracts
where sophisticated parties negotiate penalty clauses as instruments of risk allocation rather


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                       21


than mere damage estimates. English law had already moved away from the genuine pre-
estimate test in Cavendish Square Holdings v. Makdessi (2015), adopting instead a "legitimate
business interest" inquiry: a stipulated sum is enforceable if it is not extravagant or
unconscionable compared to the legitimate business interest it protects.

The Supreme Court of India, in BPL Ltd. v. Morgan Securities (2026), endorsed a similar
evolution. The Court held that where both parties are commercial entities with equal bargaining
power, a liquidated damages clause should be tested not against whether it was a genuine pre-
estimate, but whether the promisee had a legitimate business interest in enforcing performance,
and whether the stipulated sum was proportionate to that interest. The Court clarified that
Section 74 does not abolish penalty clauses altogether; rather, it subjects them to a
proportionality-and-legitimacy review. A clause that protects a real commercial interest, even
if it exceeds actual loss, may be enforceable if it satisfies this test. The Court further cautioned
that courts must not rewrite commercial bargains struck at arm's length between informed
parties.
