content.passageText:
The Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950, issued by the President of India under Article
341 of the Constitution, defines which communities are recognised as Scheduled Castes for
constitutional purposes. Paragraph 3 of that Order, as amended in 1956, provides that no person
professing a religion other than Hinduism, Sikhism, or Buddhism shall be deemed a member
of a Scheduled Caste. The practical effect of this provision is significant: a person born into a
Scheduled Caste who converts to Christianity or Islam loses the constitutionally recognised SC
status for the purposes of all legal benefits, reservations, and protections that flow from that
classification.

This has direct consequences under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, which
creates special offences and enhanced penalties for crimes committed against persons
belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The Act's protections are triggered by
the victim's status as a member of an SC or ST community. Where the victim has converted to


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                       24


a religion outside the three recognised faiths under the 1950 Order, they no longer hold SC
status in the eyes of the law, and the Act accordingly ceases to apply to offences against them.

Courts have consistently applied this framework without extending its protections by analogy.
The rationale advanced for limiting SC status to Hinduism, Sikhism, and Buddhism is that the
caste system, as a social institution rooted in hierarchical religious practice, is historically
linked to these faiths. Whether a convert continues to face social discrimination has been
treated as a separate question from whether the legal definition of SC status is satisfied. The
1950 Order has been affirmed by the Supreme Court as a valid exercise of the power conferred
by Article 341, and Parliament alone has the competence to amend it.

       (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. The court would most likely:
options:

       formal legal classification to actual social discrimination suffered.

Accept the complaint, as Sumati's caste identity remains a social reality and her
       conversion does not extinguish the discrimination she experienced.

Reject the complaint on procedural grounds but allow Sumati to refile after producing
       documentary evidence of continued social exclusion post-conversion.

Reject the complaint, since Sumati's conversion to Islam removes her from the SC
       category under Paragraph 3 of the 1950 Order, making the Act inapplicable.

content.passageText:
The Special Marriage Act, 1954, provides a secular mechanism for civil marriage in India,
enabling persons of any religion, caste, or nationality to solemnise and register their union
outside the framework of personal religious laws. The Act prescribes minimum age
requirements of twenty-one years for the male party and eighteen years for the female party at
the time of marriage.

The procedure under the Act requires the parties to give a notice of intended marriage to the
Marriage Officer of the district where either party has resided for at least thirty days before the
notice. This notice is entered in a public register and is open to inspection by any person without
payment of a fee, creating a transparency mechanism that has drawn criticism for potentially
endangering couples whose families oppose the union. Within thirty days of the notice, any
person may object to the marriage on limited grounds: namely, that the marriage would
contravene any condition specified in the Act. These conditions include age requirements,
prohibited degrees of relationship, an existing subsisting marriage of either party, and the
mental incapacity of either party. The Marriage Officer must inquire into every objection and
may refuse registration only if the objection falls within these enumerated grounds.

Once the marriage is solemnised and the Marriage Officer issues a certificate, that certificate
serves as conclusive proof of the marriage. The certificate is not merely evidence of
solemnisation; it establishes the fact of marriage with finality for all legal purposes.

An important consequence concerns succession: where a marriage is registered under the
Special Marriage Act, the succession to the parties' property, and to the property of their
children, is governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925, irrespective of the personal law that


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                         27


would otherwise apply to either party. This means that a Hindu who marries under the Special
Marriage Act is not governed by the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, in matters of inheritance.

       register their marriage under the Special Marriage Act. Preethi's family objects, arguing
       the marriage would cause social harm and the couple lacks maturity. The Marriage
       Officer should:
options:
Defer solemnisation for six months to allow both families an opportunity to present
       their objections formally through a court of competent jurisdiction.

Accept the objection since the Act permits any person to object on grounds that the
       marriage is contrary to the interests of the female party.

Reject the objection, since the grounds of social harm and immaturity are not among
       the statutory grounds for objection, but must also refuse registration because Arjun is
       below twenty-one.

Proceed with solemnisation since both parties satisfy the minimum age requirements
       and no valid statutory ground for objection has been raised.

content.passageText:
The growth of platform-based gig work in India prompted legislative action at both the central
and state levels. The Social Security Code, 2020, for the first time recognised "gig workers"
and "platform workers" as distinct categories in Indian labour law. The Code mandates that the
central government formulate welfare schemes for such workers covering life and disability
cover, health and maternity benefits, old age protection, and other benefits. The Code also
obligates aggregators, defined as digital intermediaries connecting buyers and service
providers, to contribute to a social security fund at a rate between one and two percent of their
annual turnover, as notified by the government.

Building on the central framework, the Karnataka Platform Based Gig Workers (Social
Security and Welfare) Act, 2025, introduced several distinct mechanisms. The Act establishes
a dedicated social security fund for gig workers in Karnataka. Aggregators operating in
Karnataka are required to pay a mandatory welfare fee on every transaction: the fee is capped
at one and a half percent of the transaction payout made to the gig worker, rather than being
calculated on overall turnover. This distinction is operationally significant. The Act also
imposes transparency obligations, requiring aggregators to disclose the basis of algorithmic
assignment of work, deactivation criteria, and earnings computations to workers and to a
designated state authority.

A grievance mechanism under the Karnataka Act entitles gig workers to seek redressal before
a board, with a time-bound response obligation on aggregators. Importantly, the Act contains
a set-off provision: contributions made by aggregators under the central Social Security Code
towards gig worker welfare may be set off against the welfare fee payable under the Karnataka
Act, preventing double payment for the same benefit period. This set-off operates automatically
upon verified submission of proof of central contributions to the Karnataka welfare board.
content.questionText:

       of its annual turnover to the central social security fund as required under the Social
       Security Code, 2020. In the same financial year, Karnataka's welfare board demands


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                        30


      the mandatory welfare fee under the 2025 Act. Quickride argues for a set-off. Under
      the framework described, which outcome is most consistent?
options:
Quickride may set off its verified central contributions against the Karnataka welfare
      fee, provided it submits proof of central contributions to the Karnataka board.

Quickride must pay the Karnataka welfare fee in full, since state obligations are legally
      distinct from central contributions and no set-off is permitted between them.

The set-off applies automatically without any submission requirement, since the 2025
      Act provides for self-executing relief upon the aggregator meeting the central
      obligation.

Quickride is exempt from the Karnataka welfare fee entirely because it has already
      discharged its obligations to gig workers through the central scheme.

In public employment governed by reservation policies, a recurring legal question concerns
whether a candidate from a reserved category who performs sufficiently well may be
considered for appointment against an unreserved or "open category" post, a process commonly
described as "migration." Migration occurs when a reserved category candidate's performance,
evaluated entirely on merit, places them above the last unreserved candidate in the open merit
list. In such cases, the candidate is appointed against the open category seat and the reserved
category vacancy remains available for other eligible candidates, thus enlarging the total
benefit to reserved category communities.

A distinct question arises where recruitment rules provide relaxations to reserved category
candidates at the eligibility stage. For instance, qualifying examinations such as the Teacher
Eligibility Test (TET) may prescribe a lower minimum passing threshold for SC/ST/OBC
candidates than for general category candidates. Candidates who clear the examination at the
relaxed threshold are fully eligible to participate in recruitment. The legal dispute is whether
having availed such a relaxation in qualifying marks bars a candidate from subsequently
migrating to the open category if their final selection score exceeds general category
candidates.

The Supreme Court addressed this question in Chaya v. State of Maharashtra (2026). The Court
held that a relaxation in qualifying marks affects eligibility alone, not a candidate's merit as
assessed in the main selection process. Once a candidate clears the qualifying examination,
their merit is determined independently and solely through the selection process. Accordingly,

In public employment governed by reservation policies, a recurring legal question concerns
whether a candidate from a reserved category who performs sufficiently well may be
considered for appointment against an unreserved or "open category" post, a process commonly
described as "migration." Migration occurs when a reserved category candidate's performance,
evaluated entirely on merit, places them above the last unreserved candidate in the open merit
list. In such cases, the candidate is appointed against the open category seat and the reserved
category vacancy remains available for other eligible candidates, thus enlarging the total
benefit to reserved category communities.

A distinct question arises where recruitment rules provide relaxations to reserved category
candidates at the eligibility stage. For instance, qualifying examinations such as the Teacher
Eligibility Test (TET) may prescribe a lower minimum passing threshold for SC/ST/OBC
candidates than for general category candidates. Candidates who clear the examination at the
relaxed threshold are fully eligible to participate in recruitment. The legal dispute is whether
having availed such a relaxation in qualifying marks bars a candidate from subsequently
migrating to the open category if their final selection score exceeds general category
candidates.

held that a relaxation in qualifying marks affects eligibility alone, not a candidate's merit as
assessed in the main selection process. Once a candidate clears the qualifying examination,
their merit is determined independently and solely through the selection process. Accordingly,
having used a relaxed qualifying threshold does not bar migration to the open category unless
the applicable recruitment rules expressly prohibit it. In the absence of such a prohibition,
migration remains available to any reserved category candidate whose merit in the selection
process places them ahead of the last general category candidate appointed.

content.passageText:
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, recognises several forms of mortgage, each carrying
distinct legal characteristics and enforcement mechanisms. In a simple mortgage, the
mortgagor does not deliver possession of the property but personally covenants to repay the
debt and agrees that upon default the mortgagee may cause the property to be sold. A
usufructuary mortgage transfers possession of the mortgaged property to the mortgagee,
entitling the mortgagee to receive the rents and profits until the debt is discharged; no personal
decree for the mortgage money lies under this form. A mortgage by deposit of title deeds, also
called an equitable mortgage, arises in certain specified cities where a debtor delivers
documents of title to a creditor with the intent of creating a security interest; no registration is
required for this form.

Enforcement of a mortgage typically proceeds through a suit for foreclosure, sale, or
redemption before a civil court. Courts exercising equitable jurisdiction retain inherent
authority to mould relief in mortgage matters, balancing the creditor's right to recover against
the hardship faced by the mortgagor. Statutory provisions and judicial practice recognise One
Time Settlement (OTS) schemes offered by banks and financial institutions, which allow
borrowers to settle outstanding mortgage dues at a negotiated figure, often below the book
value of the debt.

In Sumaiya Parveen v. Central Bank of India (2026), the Supreme Court was confronted with
a situation where a widow sought to avail an OTS scheme offered by the bank, but the offer
had lapsed before she could complete payment due to circumstances beyond her control. The
bank refused to extend the scheme. The Supreme Court, invoking its plenary power under
Article 142 of the Constitution to do complete justice, directed the bank to honour the OTS
arrangement on the original terms. The Court characterised its intervention as an exercise of
equitable jurisdiction available in exceptional circumstances to prevent manifest injustice.

      Under the classification and enforcement rules described, the bank may:
options:

      against the mortgagor and limits the mortgagee to extinguishing Harish's equity.

Seek both a personal decree and usufructuary possession, since simple mortgages allow
      the mortgagee to take over rents and profits in addition to pursuing the mortgagor
      personally.

Seek a personal decree and cause the property to be sold through court proceedings,
      consistent with the enforcement mechanism applicable to a simple mortgage.

Seek only a decree for sale without any personal remedy, since Harish's non-delivery
      of possession limits the bank to realising the security without further personal liability.

content.passageText:
Most people in the world eat meat, yet very few have visited a factory farm. This gap between
consumption and knowledge matters, because the conditions in industrial animal agriculture
are far removed from the pastoral images that appear on food packaging. The vast majority of
chickens, pigs, and cattle raised for food in the world today are kept in concentrated animal
feeding operations, commonly known as CAFOs. In these facilities, animals are often confined
in spaces so small that they cannot turn around, engage in natural behaviours, or avoid contact
with their own waste.
The scale of this system is staggering. Roughly 80 billion land animals are slaughtered for food
each year globally. Scientists and veterinarians broadly agree that pigs, cows, and chickens are
sentient creatures capable of experiencing pain, stress, and fear. When animals raised in
CAFOs exhibit behaviours such as feather-pecking, tail-biting, and repetitive pacing, these are
widely understood by animal behaviourists as signs of chronic stress caused by confinement
and deprivation of natural stimuli.
Defenders of industrial farming argue that it is the only way to produce enough food at prices
ordinary people can afford. They point out that modern food systems have made protein
accessible to populations that once faced serious nutritional deficits, and that improving
conditions for farm animals would inevitably raise costs and price poorer consumers out of the
market. Some also argue that because humans are omnivores by nature, there is nothing
inherently wrong with using animals for food.
Critics of this view respond that the argument from necessity is weaker than it appears. Food
systems could be reorganised to produce less meat more humanely, without necessarily making


                                      12minutestoclat.com                                        45


protein unaffordable. Many nutritionists argue that high levels of meat consumption in wealthy
countries far exceed dietary needs. The ethical question is not whether humans can eat animals,
but whether they are justified in inflicting large-scale suffering on sentient creatures for the
sake of convenience and low prices, when alternatives exist.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from "Animal Welfare and Industrial Agriculture", The
Humane Society International, and "The Ethics of What We Eat", Peter Singer and Jim
Mason.]

being redistributed equally between Rural passenger fares and Rural freight charges. Unless

the subsidy reform proposal.

children, namely Ananya, Bhuvan, and Chitra, in the ratio 5:4:3, respectively, at the time of his
retirement. He stipulated that Ananya must invest her share in a fixed deposit offering Simple
Interest at 8% per annum for 3 years, Bhuvan must invest his share in a recurring scheme
offering Compound Interest at 10% per annum, compounded annually, for 2 years, and Chitra
must invest her share in a trading venture. Chitra, instead of investing in a trading venture as

originally stipulated, used her share to purchase goods. She availed a discount of 16 " % on the

Marked Price of the goods, and the amount she paid after the discount became her Cost Price.

thus earned, Chitra lent one-third to her friend Devika at a Simple Interest of 12% per annum
for 2 years, while the remaining two-thirds she deposited in a scheme offering Compound
Interest at 20% per annum, compounded annually, for 2 years.

Bhuvan, after receiving the maturity amount at the end of 2 years, observed that the difference
between the Compound Interest he earned and the Simple Interest that would have been earned
on the same principal, at the same rate, and for the same duration, was exactly ₹320. The actual
amount invested, however, was not the same as the share originally allocated to him. At the
end of the 2 years, Chitra received the full repayment from Devika.

invested in was fraudulent. The scheme operator absconded, and Chitra recovered only her
principal amount of ₹5,000 through legal recourse; the interest component was entirely lost.
Undeterred, Chitra immediately reinvested this recovered principal of ₹5,000 in a reliable bank
fixed deposit offering Simple Interest at 15% per annum for 2 years.

must invest her share in a trading venture. Chitra, instead of investing in a trading venture as

Marked Price of the goods, and the amount she paid after the discount became her Cost Price.

thus earned, Chitra lent one-third to her friend Devika at a Simple Interest of 12% per annum
for 2 years, while the remaining two-thirds she deposited in a scheme offering Compound
Interest at 20% per annum, compounded annually, for 2 years.

ENGLISH LANGUAGE
For over 1,00,000 years, Homo Sapiens warred with the Neanderthals for supremacy — a battle
to the death, literally. Eventually, the early modern humans won out, and Neanderthals went
extinct. And that was the only story ever told. But in these millennia of co-existence, conflict
and competition weren’t the only way the two species engaged with each other. They shared
DNA, 99.7 per cent of it, practices like burying their dead, wearing jewellery, making art —
and families. A new study from the University of Oxford substantiates this claim: Humans and
Neanderthals were in love too, not just at war.


The researchers, studying the evolutionary history of kissing across species, came up with a
simple explanation for a shared oral microbe between Neanderthals and humans. Coupled with
evidence of interbreeding as late as 50,000 years ago, the researchers argue that not only did
Neanderthals, like chimps, bonobos and humans, kiss each other — but human beings too.
There has been a focus on competition — and not nearly enough on cooperation. Robert Ardrey
and Raymond Dart’s “killer ape theory” posited that war and interpersonal aggression was the
driving force behind human evolution. While cooperative competition is part of the history of
survival, this hardly tells the whole story. For instance, bonobos, along with chimps, the closest
evolutionary cousins of Homo Sapiens, privilege cooperation. Like humans, they live in
communities and their tools of choice are affection, negotiation and loyalty. In a world riveted
on differences and obsessed with the rat race, it may help to get better at love, not war.

starring-neanderthals-10375032/

'I suppose you will be getting away pretty soon, now Fall term is over, Professor,' said a person
not in the story to the Professor of Ontography, soon after they had sat down next to each other
at a feast in the hospitable hall of St James's College. The Professor was young, neat, and
precise in speech.


'Yes,' he said; 'my friends have been making me take up golf this term, and I mean to go to the
East Coast - in point of fact to Burnstow - (I dare say you know it) for a week or ten days, to
improve my game. I hope to get off tomorrow.'


'Oh, Parkins,' said his neighbour on the other side, 'if you are going to Burnstow, I wish you
would look at the site of the Templars' preceptory, and let me know if you think it would be
any good to have a dig there in the summer.'


'Certainly,' said Parkins, the Professor: 'if you will describe to me whereabouts the site is, I will
do my best to give you an idea of the lie of the land when I get back; or I could write to you
about it, if you would tell me where you are likely to be.'


'Don't trouble to do that, thanks. It's only that I'm thinking of taking my family in that direction
in the Long, and it occurred to me that, as very few of the English preceptories have ever been
properly planned, I might have an opportunity of doing something useful on offdays.'


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                           4


The Professor rather sniffed at the idea that planning a preceptory could be considered useful.
His neighbour continued: 'The site - I doubt if there is anything showing above ground - must
be down quite close to the beach now. I should think, from the map, that it must be about three-
quarters of a mile from the Globe Inn, at the north end of the town. Where are you going to
stay?'


'Well, at the Globe Inn, as a matter of fact,' said Parkins

'I suppose you will be getting away pretty soon, now Fall term is over, Professor,' said a person
not in the story to the Professor of Ontography, soon after they had sat down next to each other
at a feast in the hospitable hall of St James's College. The Professor was young, neat, and
precise in speech.

East Coast - in point of fact to Burnstow - (I dare say you know it) for a week or ten days, to
improve my game. I hope to get off tomorrow.'


'Oh, Parkins,' said his neighbour on the other side, 'if you are going to Burnstow, I wish you
would look at the site of the Templars' preceptory, and let me know if you think it would be
any good to have a dig there in the summer.'

There is more to home advantage than just the pitch. But by asking for specific kinds of wickets,
coach Gautam Gambhir and the India team management have suffered the ignominy of trying
to set a trap for the opposition, and then falling into it themselves. The defeat against South
Africa at Eden Gardens is India’s fourth loss in six home Tests — an indication of how poorly
India, under Gambhir, have played their cards. The last four losses before the most recent
downturn spanned seven years (February 2017 to January 2024). Now, we have seen four in
13 months.


Curators know local conditions best, and if left alone, they will usually try to produce a wicket
that promises good cricket. But when you start asking them to mix things up just a few days
before the game, there is a risk of things backfiring as they did at Eden. The batters, as the Test


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                          6


tour of England in June-August showed, are good enough, but if you reduce batting to a lottery,
then there are no guarantees. Yes, the batters should have done better. But this is also a young
batting unit that must be allowed to come into its own. Even the best Indian batters have
struggled at home in the last five years — with only Yashasvi Jaiswal (1,322 runs at 57.47)
averaging over 50. A doctored pitch is the last thing such a line-up needs.


Eden Gardens saw great crowds for its first Test in six years, but the match itself ended within
three days. The demand for such pitches, thus, does a disservice to spectators and the game
itself. The England series was fun because it tested the cricketers’ technique and temperament,
and most matches went the distance. India have much to introspect — in terms of both team
and pitch — and it would be a pity if an anticipated win in the next test sweeps these concerns
under the carpet.

India, along with other key markets like China and Brazil, will see a key ingredient in weight
loss drugs go off patent next year. This could lead to a drastic drop in prices as generics makers
ready plans to produce their own versions of these drugs in countries with high incidence of
obesity and associated lifestyle diseases such as diabetes. Competition is intensifying among
patent holders Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk as the expiry approaches. They are trying to shore
up market shares through aggressive price cuts, although these are unlikely to match the level
of inexpensive generics, which could sell for as little as a tenth of current prices.


The strategy is to pitch the drugs at affluent patients as a lifestyle product despite them being
available only by prescription. MNCs holding patents for anti-obesity drugs are also sealing up
arrangements with local pharmaceutical companies to widen their distribution. The idea is to


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                         8


raise product awareness in price-sensitive markets with rapid growth in obesity so that the
overall numbers make up for market share that will eventually be lost to generics. Effort is also
being made to highlight the innovators' value proposition to physicians. Some combinations
will continue to enjoy patent protection for a while longer.


Affordable slimming drugs are expected to be wildly popular in a country that is battling its
bulge unsuccessfully. A combination of rising affluence and inadequate health awareness
makes India a key market for anti-obesity pills, even if they are not sold over the counter. Some
degree of caution may be called for by Indian drug makers eagerly anticipating a blockbuster
pill going off-patent. There is restraint built into the production process - these drugs are not
easy to replicate. But regulators may have to consider more proactive messaging that while
drugs to lose weight may be within reach, there is no substitute for exercise. The morning walk
will do you more good than popping a pill to confuse your brain about hunger. But that's
another ask and task.

Since the advent of Bitcoin, and the subsequent proliferation of cryptocurrencies, there have
been concerns over the regulatory challenges posed by the crypto universe. Over the years,


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                      10


numerous instances of fraud, scams and other illicit activities have come to light. For instance,
in 2022, FTX, a cryptocurrency exchange, collapsed, and its founder Sam Bankman-Fried was
convicted for fraud and conspiracy to launder money. In 2023, Changpeng Zhao, founder of
Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, pleaded guilty to violating US anti-money
laundering laws. Crypto exchanges have been levied fines, penalties, and settlements totalling
more than $5.8 billion, according to an analysis by the International Consortium of
Investigative Journalists (ICIJ). In India, between 2024 and 2025, the Financial Intelligence
Unit has levied fines on Binance (Rs 18.82 crore), ByBit (Rs 9.27 crore) and KuCoin (Rs 34.5
lakh) — for violating anti-money laundering laws. Crypto regulation is fragmented. Taking
advantage of this grey zone, crypto exchanges have become hubs for dirty money to cross
national borders as shown by an investigation by this paper, in partnership with the ICIJ. This
is a matter of grave concern.


A shadow economy has emerged worldwide, and India is no exception. The anonymity that
crypto offers along with the ease of transferring across borders makes this a widely preferred
medium. For instance, following the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the World Economic Forum
noted concerns about the use of crypto to evade international sanctions. In addition to hawala
deals, even money stolen by cybercrimes is being channelled through these routes — as per an
estimate, Rs 623 crore has been funneled.


India, with more than 100 million users, is a big crypto market. However, there is no
overarching crypto framework that regulates the sector. Crypto exchanges, wallet providers
and others must register with the Financial Intelligence Unit. But those who have done so
account for only a small proportion of the universe. As this space grows — from $2.6 billion
to $15 billion by 2035, as per an estimate — there is need for policy clarity. The guardrails
need to be put in place.

content.passageText:
Since the advent of Bitcoin, and the subsequent proliferation of cryptocurrencies, there have
been concerns over the regulatory challenges posed by the crypto universe. Over the years,


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                      10


numerous instances of fraud, scams and other illicit activities have come to light. For instance,
in 2022, FTX, a cryptocurrency exchange, collapsed, and its founder Sam Bankman-Fried was
convicted for fraud and conspiracy to launder money. In 2023, Changpeng Zhao, founder of
Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, pleaded guilty to violating US anti-money
laundering laws. Crypto exchanges have been levied fines, penalties, and settlements totalling
more than $5.8 billion, according to an analysis by the International Consortium of
Investigative Journalists (ICIJ). In India, between 2024 and 2025, the Financial Intelligence
Unit has levied fines on Binance (Rs 18.82 crore), ByBit (Rs 9.27 crore) and KuCoin (Rs 34.5
lakh) — for violating anti-money laundering laws. Crypto regulation is fragmented. Taking
advantage of this grey zone, crypto exchanges have become hubs for dirty money to cross
national borders as shown by an investigation by this paper, in partnership with the ICIJ. This
is a matter of grave concern.


A shadow economy has emerged worldwide, and India is no exception. The anonymity that
crypto offers along with the ease of transferring across borders makes this a widely preferred
medium. For instance, following the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the World Economic Forum
noted concerns about the use of crypto to evade international sanctions. In addition to hawala
deals, even money stolen by cybercrimes is being channelled through these routes — as per an
estimate, Rs 623 crore has been funneled.


India, with more than 100 million users, is a big crypto market. However, there is no
overarching crypto framework that regulates the sector. Crypto exchanges, wallet providers
and others must register with the Financial Intelligence Unit. But those who have done so
account for only a small proportion of the universe. As this space grows — from $2.6 billion
to $15 billion by 2035, as per an estimate — there is need for policy clarity. The guardrails
need to be put in place.
SOURCE:https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/editorials/as-dirty-money-flows-through-
crypto-markets-raise-the-guardrails-10373240/

misgivings with the group were well established since 2021. At the root of Abu Dhabi’s
dissatisfaction was that its production quota, which determines how much oil each member
produces in a given month, had continuously lagged state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil

content.passageText:
LEGAL REASONING

Offences against property in the Indian Penal Code, now mirrored in the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, operate along a graduated scale of severity. Extortion, robbery, and dacoity form a
connected chain, with each successive offence incorporating the elements of the one before it
and adding a further aggravating ingredient.

Extortion, under the IPC, is constituted by three cumulative elements: the accused must
intentionally put a person in fear of injury, that fear must be induced so as to cause the person
to deliver property or a valuable security, and the delivery must be in consequence of that fear.
The fear need not be of bodily harm; a threat to injure reputation or to cause wrongful loss to


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                        20


any person in whom the threatened party is interested suffices. Crucially, no immediate
confrontation is required — the threat may be communicated remotely, and the offence is
complete the moment the person parts with the property out of apprehension, whether or not
the accused is physically present.

Robbery is defined as theft or extortion in an aggravated form. Theft becomes robbery when,
in order to commit theft, or in carrying away or attempting to carry away property, the offender
voluntarily causes or attempts to cause death, hurt, or wrongful restraint to any person, or puts
any person in fear of instant death, instant hurt, or instant wrongful restraint. Extortion becomes
robbery when the offender, at the time of committing the extortion, is present in person and
puts the victim in fear of instant injury. The key distinction from ordinary extortion is the
element of immediacy and the physical presence of the perpetrator.

Dacoity elevates the offence further: it occurs when five or more persons conjointly commit or
attempt to commit robbery. Every person who is one of the five or more persons assembled for
that purpose is deemed to have committed dacoity. This constructive or joint liability rule is
unsparing: a member of the assembly who neither wields a weapon nor participates actively in
the taking is still guilty of dacoity, because the law attributes the collective act to each
participant individually. The rationale is deterrence — the presence of large numbers amplifies
the terror and coercive capacity of the group beyond what any individual could achieve.

       shopkeeper, frightened, decides to comply, but when he opens his safe, it is completely
       empty. He has no money to leave out. Ranveer never arrives at the store. Which of the
       following most accurately captures Ranveer's criminal exposure under the provisions
       governing robbery?
options:
Robbery is established since Ranveer put the shopkeeper in fear of injury and intended
       to obtain property, satisfying the core ingredients of an aggravated offence.

Extortion is established since Ranveer intentionally induced fear of injury to reputation
       in order to cause the shopkeeper to deliver property, and the offence is complete even
       though no property was actually delivered, since the shopkeeper's intention to comply
       is sufficient for delivery.

No offence under robbery is established since Ranveer was not physically present, did
      not cause fear of instant injury, and no property was delivered; the essential ingredients
      of robbery are entirely absent.

Dacoity is established since Ranveer's threat was severe enough to constitute the kind
      of coercive force that the law attributes to group offences, even when committed alone.

content.passageText:
LEGAL REASONING

Offences against property in the Indian Penal Code, now mirrored in the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, operate along a graduated scale of severity. Extortion, robbery, and dacoity form a
connected chain, with each successive offence incorporating the elements of the one before it
and adding a further aggravating ingredient.

Extortion, under the IPC, is constituted by three cumulative elements: the accused must
intentionally put a person in fear of injury, that fear must be induced so as to cause the person
to deliver property or a valuable security, and the delivery must be in consequence of that fear.
The fear need not be of bodily harm; a threat to injure reputation or to cause wrongful loss to


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                        20


any person in whom the threatened party is interested suffices. Crucially, no immediate
confrontation is required — the threat may be communicated remotely, and the offence is
complete the moment the person parts with the property out of apprehension, whether or not
the accused is physically present.

Robbery is defined as theft or extortion in an aggravated form. Theft becomes robbery when,
in order to commit theft, or in carrying away or attempting to carry away property, the offender
voluntarily causes or attempts to cause death, hurt, or wrongful restraint to any person, or puts
any person in fear of instant death, instant hurt, or instant wrongful restraint. Extortion becomes
robbery when the offender, at the time of committing the extortion, is present in person and
puts the victim in fear of instant injury. The key distinction from ordinary extortion is the
element of immediacy and the physical presence of the perpetrator.

Dacoity elevates the offence further: it occurs when five or more persons conjointly commit or
attempt to commit robbery. Every person who is one of the five or more persons assembled for
that purpose is deemed to have committed dacoity. This constructive or joint liability rule is
unsparing: a member of the assembly who neither wields a weapon nor participates actively in
the taking is still guilty of dacoity, because the law attributes the collective act to each
participant individually. The rationale is deterrence — the presence of large numbers amplifies
the terror and coercive capacity of the group beyond what any individual could achieve.

Section 494 of the Indian Penal Code, re-enacted as Section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
penalises a person who contracts a second marriage during the lifetime of a living spouse,
provided the first marriage subsists and has not been dissolved by a competent court. The
offence is premised on the second marriage being void by reason of the first. This dependency
on voidness is the provision's most critical feature: if the second marriage is not rendered void
by the applicable personal law, the criminal provision is not attracted.

For Muslim males governed by Muslim personal law, the plurality of marriages is permitted,
subject to the conditions of equal treatment and financial capacity recognised by that law. A
second marriage contracted by a Muslim husband is not void under Muslim personal law; it is
treated as legally valid. Because the second marriage is not void, the predicate for the criminal
offence of bigamy under Section 494 IPC or Section 82 BNS is absent, and no prosecution will
lie.

The contrast with Hindu law is stark. Under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a second marriage
contracted during the subsistence of a first marriage is null and void, regardless of
circumstances. This absolute prohibition makes a Hindu's second marriage the paradigm case
for bigamy under the penal provision.

       Courts have also recognised that the High Court's inherent power under Section 528 of the
       BNSS (previously Section 482 CrPC) to quash criminal proceedings may be exercised
       where the complaint discloses no offence — as where a Muslim husband's second marriage
       is the subject of a bigamy complaint that is legally untenable. However, the power under
       Section 528 BNSS is not the focus of this passage; the substantive law is that Muslim
       personal law's position on polygamy directly determines whether the criminal offence of
       bigamy is attracted, by negating the essential ingredient of the second marriage being void.

content.passageText:
Partnership under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 is the relation between persons who have
agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. This
definition reveals four indispensable elements: an agreement between two or more persons, a
business being carried on, sharing of profits, and mutual agency. Mutual agency is the crucial
structural element: each partner is simultaneously the principal who can be bound by the acts
of co-partners, and the agent who can bind those co-partners. A mere sharing of profits is not,
by itself, conclusive evidence of a partnership; the mutual agency element must be present.

Partners stand in a fiduciary relationship with one another. Each partner is required to be just
and faithful to the firm, to render true accounts, and to account for any private profit derived
from any transaction connected with the firm or from any use of the firm's property or goodwill.
If a partner, without the consent of co-partners, carries on a business of the same nature
competing with that of the firm, that partner must account to the firm for all profits made. These
fiduciary obligations persist throughout the duration of the partnership and bind both active
and dormant partners equally.

Toward third parties, partners bear joint and several liability for all acts of the firm done while
they were partners. A third party who suffers loss may sue any one partner or all of them, and
recovery from one partner does not extinguish the obligations of the rest. Registration of a firm


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                         27


does not affect this liability toward outsiders; it does, however, affect the firm's ability to
enforce its own claims in court, as an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties to enforce
contract rights, though this disability does not bar third parties from suing the firm.

When a partner retires, they continue to be liable to third parties for acts of the firm until public
notice of retirement is given. Without such notice, persons who had previously dealt with the
firm may continue to treat the retiring partner as still a member and hold her liable for
subsequent obligations. Dissolution of the firm, by contrast, terminates the firm's existence
entirely, and assets must be applied in a prescribed order: first to discharge liabilities to third
parties, then to repay partners' advances, and finally to return capital contributions, with any
residue shared in the profit-sharing ratio.

        delivers goods worth two lakh rupees on credit. The firm defaults. Deepak sues Aditya
        alone for the full amount. Aditya argues he is liable for only his one-third share, and
        that as the firm is unregistered, no suit can be maintained. Identify the correct legal
        position.
options:
Deepak cannot recover from Aditya alone, because joint liability requires all partners
        to be simultaneously impleaded, and a suit against fewer than all partners is
        procedurally incompetent.

Deepak can recover the full amount from Aditya alone, since the joint and several
        liability of partners toward third parties is unaffected by the firm's registration status
        and Aditya bears the entire debt.

Deepak's suit must fail because an unregistered firm and its partners enjoy a complete
        immunity from suits for the recovery of debts arising from transactions conducted by
        the firm.

Aditya is personally liable for only a proportionate share of the debt, since joint liability
        in partnership means each partner's exposure is capped at the fraction corresponding to
        her profit-sharing ratio.

      to capture profits made before discovery.

content.passageText:
Partnership under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 is the relation between persons who have
agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. This
definition reveals four indispensable elements: an agreement between two or more persons, a
business being carried on, sharing of profits, and mutual agency. Mutual agency is the crucial
structural element: each partner is simultaneously the principal who can be bound by the acts
of co-partners, and the agent who can bind those co-partners. A mere sharing of profits is not,
by itself, conclusive evidence of a partnership; the mutual agency element must be present.

Partners stand in a fiduciary relationship with one another. Each partner is required to be just
and faithful to the firm, to render true accounts, and to account for any private profit derived
from any transaction connected with the firm or from any use of the firm's property or goodwill.
If a partner, without the consent of co-partners, carries on a business of the same nature
competing with that of the firm, that partner must account to the firm for all profits made. These
fiduciary obligations persist throughout the duration of the partnership and bind both active
and dormant partners equally.

Toward third parties, partners bear joint and several liability for all acts of the firm done while
they were partners. A third party who suffers loss may sue any one partner or all of them, and
recovery from one partner does not extinguish the obligations of the rest. Registration of a firm


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                         27


does not affect this liability toward outsiders; it does, however, affect the firm's ability to
enforce its own claims in court, as an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties to enforce
contract rights, though this disability does not bar third parties from suing the firm.

When a partner retires, they continue to be liable to third parties for acts of the firm until public
notice of retirement is given. Without such notice, persons who had previously dealt with the
firm may continue to treat the retiring partner as still a member and hold her liable for
subsequent obligations. Dissolution of the firm, by contrast, terminates the firm's existence
entirely, and assets must be applied in a prescribed order: first to discharge liabilities to third
parties, then to repay partners' advances, and finally to return capital contributions, with any
residue shared in the profit-sharing ratio.

The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 established Lok Adalats as a statutory mechanism
for alternative dispute resolution. The framework is tiered: the National Legal Services
Authority operates at the apex, the State Legal Services Authorities function at the state level,
District Legal Services Authorities operate at the district level, and Taluk Legal Services
Committees serve sub-district areas. Each level is empowered to organise Lok Adalats for
disputes falling within its territorial and subject-matter jurisdiction.

Lok Adalats have jurisdiction over two categories of disputes. First, they may take up matters
pending before a court if both parties consent to a reference. Second, they may address pre-
litigation disputes where no court proceedings have been initiated, provided again that both
parties agree to participate. One category of disputes is, however, expressly excluded: offences
that are not compoundable under any law in force cannot be settled before a Lok Adalat. This
restriction reflects the legislative policy that where the State has determined that private
settlement of an offence is impermissible, the Lok Adalat mechanism cannot be used to
circumvent that determination.

Once a Lok Adalat arrives at a settlement, the award it records is deemed to be a decree of a
civil court and is final and binding on the parties. Critically, no appeal lies from a Lok Adalat
award to any court. The only recourse available to a party dissatisfied with the outcome is to
treat the settlement as not having occurred and to pursue the original remedy before the
appropriate forum. This finality, combined with the absence of court fees on Lok Adalat
proceedings, makes it an attractive mode of resolution.

Permanent Lok Adalats are a specialised institution established under Chapter VI-A of the Act
for disputes relating to public utility services, which include transport, insurance, supply of
power, and similar essential services. Unlike ordinary Lok Adalats, a Permanent Lok Adalat is
empowered to impose a settlement on the parties even if one party objects, provided the dispute
relates to a public utility service. This power to make binding determinations without bilateral
consent distinguishes Permanent Lok Adalats structurally from the consensus-based ordinary
Lok Adalat.

        payee approach the District Legal Services Authority seeking settlement through a Lok
        Adalat. The magistrate objects that the case has already been taken up for trial. Which
        of the following is correct?

options:
The reference to Lok Adalat is incompetent because once a case is set down for trial,
      the trial court retains exclusive jurisdiction and no alternative forum may receive the
      dispute during the pendency of trial proceedings.

The reference is maintainable only if the payee withdraws the original complaint before
      the Lok Adalat is convened, since the simultaneous operation of two forums on the
      same subject matter is jurisdictionally impermissible.

The reference is maintainable, since Lok Adalats may take up matters pending before
      a court on the consent of both parties, and the offence of cheque dishonour is
      compoundable, removing the statutory bar.

The reference is not maintainable because cheque-dishonour cases are criminal matters,
      and Lok Adalats are constitutionally restricted to civil disputes, being a creature of
      statute with no authority over offences.

A Lok Adalat issues an award directing an insurance company to pay a claimant two
      lakh rupees in settlement of a motor accident claim. The insurance company later
      contends that the award was reached under a misapprehension and files an appeal before
      the High Court. The claimant seeks dismissal of the appeal. What should the court hold?
options:
The appeal must be dismissed, since awards of Lok Adalats are deemed decrees of a
      civil court and the statute expressly bars any appeal from such awards, regardless of the
      ground on which the award is challenged.

The appeal is maintainable on the ground of fundamental error, since an award obtained
      through misapprehension is voidable and the court's supervisory jurisdiction under
      Article 227 of the Constitution is unaffected by the bar on ordinary appeals.

The appeal is maintainable because the prohibition on appeals from Lok Adalat awards
      applies only to awards made in pre-litigation disputes, not to matters referred to Lok
      Adalat after court proceedings were initiated.

The insurance company may challenge the award by way of review rather than appeal,
      and the High Court has jurisdiction to set aside an award on a review petition even when
      the statute bars a formal appeal.

      brought before a Permanent Lok Adalat. The company refuses to accept the proposed

      related dispute to a Lok Adalat. The Lok Adalat holds three sessions but the parties fail
      to reach any agreement. Neither party has signed any settlement deed. Vikram then files
      a suit in civil court for recovery of wages. The employer objects that the Lok Adalat

The objection is valid, since a Lok Adalat is a court of competent jurisdiction under the
      statute and any dispute it hears and determines, even without a formal award, operates
      as a final adjudication between the parties.

The objection is not valid, since no award was reached; where a Lok Adalat fails to
      produce a settlement, the parties retain the right to seek relief before the appropriate
      forum as if the Lok Adalat proceedings had not occurred.

      the failed Lok Adalat proceedings to shift the burden of proof to Vikram for
      demonstrating why the earlier settlement attempt did not conclude.

      normally be waived in Lok Adalat proceedings before the civil suit is admitted, as a
      precondition for transferring the dispute to the court.

         sought to be referred to a Lok Adalat by one of the accused, who claims the victim is

The reference is permissible because the consent of both the victim and the accused is
         sufficient to invoke the jurisdiction of a Lok Adalat for any pending criminal matter,
         overriding the prosecution's objection.

         Adalat jurisdiction over criminal matters cannot be invoked.

content.passageText:
The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 codifies the right of a Hindu wife to claim
maintenance from her husband. However, the statute is not the exclusive avenue through which
such a right may be enforced. The Kerala High Court, in a ruling delivered in January 2026,
reaffirmed and elaborated the principle that a Hindu wife's right to maintenance operates
independently of, and outside, the HAMA framework. She may claim maintenance dehors the
statute — that is, by invoking her common law rights as recognised and preserved by the courts.

The significance of this ruling lies in its extension to the husband's immovable property. The
court held that a Hindu wife is entitled to claim maintenance directly from her husband's
immovable property, not merely from his personal income or movable assets. Once
proceedings for maintenance are instituted, the wife's right to maintenance attaches as a charge
on the husband's immovable property from the date of initiation of those proceedings. This
converts the wife's personal right against her husband into a right in rem against a specific
asset.

The consequence of the right attaching as a charge is highly significant for third parties dealing
with that property. Any transfer of the husband's immovable property after the maintenance


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                         34


proceedings have been initiated is subject to and cannot defeat the wife's pre-existing charge.
A purchaser who acquires the property after the initiation of proceedings takes it encumbered
by the wife's charge, even if the transfer is made for valuable consideration and even if the
purchaser is otherwise unaware of the matrimonial dispute.

This ruling has implications for the general law of property in family disputes. It prevents a
husband from defeating maintenance claims by transferring assets during litigation. Courts
have historically been watchful of property disposals designed to defraud or prejudice a
maintenance claimant, and the recognition of an automatic charge from the date of institution
reinforces that protective policy. The decision represents a significant convergence of personal
law rights with proprietary remedies.
content.questionText:
Kavitha files an application for maintenance against her husband Jayaram before a
       family court in January. In March, without Kavitha's knowledge, Jayaram sells his
       residential plot to Suresh, a bona fide purchaser for full market value who has no
       knowledge of the maintenance proceedings. Suresh later discovers the proceedings had
       commenced in January. Which of the following is the most accurate statement of the
       legal position?
options:
Suresh holds the property free of Kavitha's charge, because his acquisition was for
       valuable consideration without prior knowledge of the charge, and the law of bona fide
       purchase protects him from encumbrances of which he had no notice.

Kavitha's charge is defeated because it had not been registered at the time of Suresh's
       purchase, and under the Transfer of Property Act, an unregistered charge on immovable
       property is void against a subsequent registered transferee.

Kavitha can recover maintenance only from Jayaram personally and not from the
       property in Suresh's hands, since the charge attaches to Jayaram's right to the proceeds
       of sale and cannot follow the property into the hands of a third party.

Suresh takes the property subject to Kavitha's charge, because the charge attaches from
       the date proceedings were initiated and any subsequent transfer of the property,
       regardless of the purchaser's knowledge, cannot extinguish that charge.

Nandita files for maintenance in February. In April, her husband Prasad gifts a plot of
      land to his brother Rajan. In July, the court grants Nandita a maintenance order. Rajan
      argues the gift was made before the maintenance order was passed and is therefore
      unaffected. Which of the following is correct?

Rajan's argument succeeds, since the wife's charge on immovable property crystallises
      only at the moment the maintenance order is formally passed by the court and cannot
      retroactively encumber earlier transfers.

      that occurred between the date of gift and the date of the court order.

Rajan's argument fails, because the charge in favour of Nandita attached to the property
      from the date of initiation of the maintenance proceedings in February, and the April
      gift transferred the plot already encumbered by that charge.

Rajan's argument succeeds only if he can demonstrate he was unaware of the
      maintenance proceedings in February, since a transferee with no knowledge of pending
      proceedings cannot be bound by a charge that had not been publicly recorded.

content.passageText:
The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 codifies the right of a Hindu wife to claim
maintenance from her husband. However, the statute is not the exclusive avenue through which
such a right may be enforced. The Kerala High Court, in a ruling delivered in January 2026,
reaffirmed and elaborated the principle that a Hindu wife's right to maintenance operates
independently of, and outside, the HAMA framework. She may claim maintenance dehors the
statute — that is, by invoking her common law rights as recognised and preserved by the courts.

The significance of this ruling lies in its extension to the husband's immovable property. The
court held that a Hindu wife is entitled to claim maintenance directly from her husband's
immovable property, not merely from his personal income or movable assets. Once
proceedings for maintenance are instituted, the wife's right to maintenance attaches as a charge
on the husband's immovable property from the date of initiation of those proceedings. This
converts the wife's personal right against her husband into a right in rem against a specific
asset.

The consequence of the right attaching as a charge is highly significant for third parties dealing
with that property. Any transfer of the husband's immovable property after the maintenance


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                         34


proceedings have been initiated is subject to and cannot defeat the wife's pre-existing charge.
A purchaser who acquires the property after the initiation of proceedings takes it encumbered
by the wife's charge, even if the transfer is made for valuable consideration and even if the
purchaser is otherwise unaware of the matrimonial dispute.

This ruling has implications for the general law of property in family disputes. It prevents a
husband from defeating maintenance claims by transferring assets during litigation. Courts
have historically been watchful of property disposals designed to defraud or prejudice a
maintenance claimant, and the recognition of an automatic charge from the date of institution
reinforces that protective policy. The decision represents a significant convergence of personal
law rights with proprietary remedies.

      husband Tarun initiates insolvency proceedings and a resolution professional is
      appointed. The resolution plan, approved in December, includes the sale of Tarun's
      immovable property to discharge creditors. Sunita seeks priority for her maintenance
      charge over secured creditors. What is the most legally defensible position based on the
      principles in the passage?
options:
Sunita's charge takes priority over all other claims, including secured creditors, because
      a matrimonial maintenance charge is a statutory charge of a superior nature that
      overrides commercial security interests as a matter of public policy.

Sunita's charge attaches to the property from June, but whether it takes priority over
      secured creditors depends on the priority rules under insolvency law, which
      independently govern the ranking of claims and may override the maintenance charge.

Sunita forfeits her charge on the immovable property upon the commencement of
      insolvency proceedings, since insolvency law vests all assets in the resolution estate
      free of encumbrances arising from personal law proceedings.

Sunita's charge is extinguished because the appointment of a resolution professional
      operates as an automatic stay on all charges created by personal law proceedings
      commenced before or after the insolvency petition was filed.

content.passageText:
The Right to Information Act, 2005 was conceived as a transparency statute, creating a
presumption in favour of disclosure and placing the burden on public authorities to justify
withholding information. Section 8 of the Act contains exemptions from the obligation to
furnish information. Among the most frequently invoked was Section 8(1)(j), which exempted
personal information from disclosure where such information had no nexus with any public
activity or interest, or where its disclosure would cause unwarranted invasion of the privacy of
an individual.

A critical feature of Section 8(1)(j) as originally enacted was the proviso that the Public
Information Officer, or the Central or State Information Commission on appeal, could order
disclosure of personal information if satisfied that the larger public interest justified disclosure.
This proviso operated as a proportionality mechanism: disclosure of otherwise private
information could be compelled if the public benefit of exposure outweighed the individual's
privacy interest. This balance reflected the foundational tension between the right to
information and the right to privacy.

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 fundamentally altered this equilibrium. Section
44(3) of the DPDPA amended Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act by removing the proviso that had
permitted disclosure in the larger public interest. As a consequence, personal information is
now categorically exempt from disclosure, and no officer or authority retains the power to order
its disclosure on public interest grounds. The proportionality test, which once required a
contextual weighing of competing interests, has been replaced by what amounts to a near-
absolute exemption.

This amendment has attracted considerable commentary from transparency advocates, who
argue that it fundamentally undermines the accountability function of the RTI Act, particularly
in cases where personal information of public officials is sought in connection with their
official conduct. Critics contend that the removal of the public interest override eliminates the
legal basis for disclosing asset declarations, financial relationships, and other information that,
while personal in form, is material to democratic accountability. Supporters of the amendment


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                          38


argue that it brings the RTI framework into alignment with the stronger privacy protections the
DPDPA is designed to guarantee.
content.questionText:
A journalist files an RTI application seeking the details of a senior civil servant's foreign
       travel expenditure paid from public funds. The public information officer cites the
       amended Section 8(1)(j) to deny the request, arguing it constitutes personal
       information. The journalist argues that expenditure from public funds is not purely
       personal. Which of the following most accurately states the legal position under the
       amended provision?
options:
The amendment creates a near-absolute exemption for personal information by
       removing the public interest override; if the information is classified as personal by the
       authority, no mechanism within the RTI Act presently allows disclosure to be
       compelled on public interest grounds.

Foreign travel expenditure from public funds is categorically excluded from the
       personal information exemption because it constitutes official conduct, and the
       exemption under amended Section 8(1)(j) applies only to information unconnected to
       the exercise of official functions.

The journalist may still succeed by invoking the proportionality doctrine developed in
       constitutional jurisprudence, which overrides statutory exemptions when disclosure is
       necessary to vindicate fundamental rights of a democratic society.

The amendment does not affect disclosure of financial information, since the DPDPA's
       definition of personal data expressly excludes information relating to monetary
       transactions conducted in an official capacity on behalf of the state.

       that disclosure of the requested personal details of a public official would serve a
       significant public interest in accountability. Under the pre-amendment RTI Act, the
       commissioner would have ordered disclosure. Under the amended provision, what
       authority does the commissioner retain?

      exemption for personal information is now categorical within the RTI framework.

      determination under Article 226, which preserves the power to compel disclosure that
      the legislature has withdrawn from administrative authorities.

Six courtrooms in a district court complex labelled A, B, C, D, E, and F, each contain an
analogue wall clock. All six clocks were accurately synchronised on a designated date known

time. The annual filing deadline for a major commercial dispute falls on a Sunday. Reset Day

of Clock A's rate of gain and Clock D's rate of gain, both expressed in minutes per hour.

content.passageText:
The last decade has seen a dramatic shift in who leads humanity’s ambitions beyond Earth. For
most of the twentieth century, space exploration was the exclusive domain of governments,
driven by the geopolitical contest between the United States and the Soviet Union. That era has
given way to something quite different: a landscape in which private companies are not merely
contractors for government agencies but independent pioneers charting their own trajectories.


The most visible symbol of this change is the emergence of companies like SpaceX, which has
not only reduced the cost of launching satellites to a fraction of what it once was but has also
revived the idea of human spaceflight as something other than a government programme. By
developing reusable rockets, SpaceX has fundamentally changed the economics of the industry.
A launch that once cost upward of two hundred million dollars can now be conducted for a
fraction of that sum, opening space to a range of users — scientific, commercial, and
governmental — who previously could not afford it.


Supporters of this commercialisation argue that private competition drives innovation faster
and more efficiently than government bureaucracies ever could. They point to the compressed
timelines and iterative design processes that have allowed SpaceX to achieve in years what
traditional contractors took decades to accomplish. Critics, however, raise legitimate concerns.
Space is increasingly congested, with the rapid deployment of large satellite constellations
threatening to create so much debris that certain low-Earth orbits could become unusable — a
scenario known as Kessler Syndrome. Regulatory frameworks designed for an era of infrequent
launches are struggling to keep pace.


There are also deeper questions about equity and the long-term governance of space. Who owns
the resources mined from asteroids or the moon? Which nations have jurisdiction over private
activities conducted beyond Earth’s atmosphere? The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 prohibits


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                       46


nations from claiming sovereignty over celestial bodies, but it was written long before private
companies became capable of extracting resources from them. As the commercial space sector
grows, these unresolved legal and ethical questions grow with it, and the urgency of addressing
them becomes harder to defer.
content.questionText: Which of the following best states the main conclusion of the passage?
options:
Private companies like SpaceX have made space travel cheaper, which proves that
          governments should no longer be involved in space exploration at all.

The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 provides a comprehensive and sufficient legal
          framework for managing the challenges posed by the growth of commercial
          spaceflight.

The rise of the private space sector has transformed the economics of spaceflight but
          has also created significant regulatory, legal, and equity challenges that remain
          unresolved.

Kessler Syndrome is an inevitable consequence of satellite deployment, and no
          regulatory framework can prevent low-Earth orbits from becoming unusable in the
          near future.

content.passageText:
Antibiotics are among the most important medical discoveries of the twentieth century. Since
Alexander Fleming observed that a mould called Penicillium was killing bacteria in his


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                        48


laboratory in 1928, these drugs have saved hundreds of millions of lives by making previously
fatal infections treatable. Yet the very mechanism that makes antibiotics effective — their
ability to kill bacteria — is now being undermined by the bacteria themselves. Through a
process of natural selection, bacteria that survive antibiotic treatment pass on resistance genes
to their offspring, gradually rendering drugs that once worked reliably ineffective.


The scale of this problem is alarming. The World Health Organisation has listed antimicrobial
resistance as one of the greatest threats to global health, food security, and development. Drug-
resistant infections already kill an estimated 1.27 million people globally each year, and
projections suggest that without intervention, this number could reach ten million annually by
2050 — surpassing cancer as a leading cause of death. The problem is compounded by the fact
that developing new antibiotics is enormously costly and commercially unattractive: bacteria
evolve resistance relatively quickly, meaning a newly developed drug may have a short
commercial lifespan, discouraging pharmaceutical investment.


Human behaviour is a major driver of the crisis. The inappropriate prescription of antibiotics
for viral infections — against which they have no effect — allows bacteria to develop resistance
without any corresponding therapeutic benefit. In many parts of the world, antibiotics are
available over the counter without a prescription, further accelerating inappropriate use. The
agricultural sector is also implicated: antibiotics are widely used in livestock farming, both to
treat disease and to promote growth, and resistant bacteria from animals can spread to humans
through the food supply and direct contact.


Addressing antibiotic resistance requires a coordinated response. Stewardship programmes that
restrict antibiotic prescribing to cases where they are genuinely needed have shown promising
results. Investment in research for new drugs and alternative treatments, such as bacteriophage
therapy, is urgently needed. And international cooperation is essential, because resistant
bacteria respect no borders.

          cause of the antibiotic resistance crisis and must be resolved before any other measure
          can succeed.

Antibiotic resistance is an inevitable consequence of natural selection and cannot be
          meaningfully slowed regardless of changes in human behaviour or prescribing
          practices.

DATA INTERPRETATION

According to the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) 2022–23, women constitute only 28 per
cent of the workforce in India's organised urban manufacturing sector. Despite their
participation, a substantial gender wage gap persists. On average, a male worker earns ₹520
per day, while a female worker earns ₹364 per day, resulting in a daily wage gap of ₹156. Over
a standard working year of 300 days, this translates into an annual earnings deficit of ₹46,800
for the average female worker.

The disparity is evident across different forms of employment. Among skilled workers, male
employees earn an average of ₹680 per day, compared with ₹476 per day earned by female
workers, resulting in a difference of ₹204. A similar pattern is observed among contract
workers: men earn ₹410 per day, while women earn ₹287, resulting in a wage gap of ₹123.
These figures indicate that wage inequality is not confined to a particular category of workers
but exists across the manufacturing workforce.

Regional differences further highlight the extent of the issue. Maharashtra records the highest
gender wage gap among organised manufacturing workers at 41 per cent, followed by Tamil
Nadu at 38 per cent. In contrast, Odisha reports the narrowest gap at 8 per cent, with male
workers earning ₹323. Adjusted for the State's Consumer Price Index (CPI) for industrial
workers, the effective annual income deficit for a female skilled worker in Maharashtra exceeds
₹75,000.

Income inequality is even more pronounced among the self-employed. In 2023, male self-
employed manufacturing workers earned 3.1 times as much as their female counterparts in
similar enterprises. Although the gender wage gap among regular wage workers narrowed from
42 per cent in 2019 to 30 per cent in 2023, significant disparities persist. Consequently, gender-
based wage inequality remains a persistent structural challenge across India's urban
manufacturing economy.

Zenith Consulting LLP employs professionals across four departments: Strategy, Analytics,
Operations, and Finance in the ratio 1:3:4:2. The current total headcount of the firm is a
multiple of 100 that lies strictly between 400 and 600, and the number of employees in the
Analytics department is strictly greater than 120 but strictly less than 200.

Three years ago, the firm's total headcount was lower than its present strength. The ratio of
male to female employees at that time was 3:1. Since then, the firm has hired additional staff
exclusively from the female pool. These new hires increased the total headcount by 25%. As a
direct consequence, the proportion of female employees in the current workforce rose to
exactly 40%.

The firm follows a department wise average annual salary structure (in Rs. lakhs) for each
department: Strategy employees earn Rs. 12 lakhs, Analytics employees earn Rs. 14 lakhs,
Operations employees earn Rs. 9 lakhs, and Finance employees earn Rs. 10 lakhs. Individual
employee salaries within a department may vary, but the departmental averages remain as
stated. At the end of the fiscal year, the firm distributed a total performance bonus of Rs. 55


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                     54


lakhs. This bonus was allocated to each department strictly in proportion to that department's
contribution to the firm's total annual salary expenditure.

decided that this revision would be achieved solely by increasing the salaries of Finance
department employees, while the salaries of all other departments remained unchanged.

multiple of 100 that lies strictly between 400 and 600, and the number of employees in the
Analytics department is strictly greater than 120 but strictly less than 200.

Three years ago, the firm's total headcount was lower than its present strength. The ratio of
male to female employees at that time was 3:1. Since then, the firm has hired additional staff
exclusively from the female pool. These new hires increased the total headcount by 25%. As a
direct consequence, the proportion of female employees in the current workforce rose to
exactly 40%.

The firm follows a department wise average annual salary structure (in Rs. lakhs) for each
department: Strategy employees earn Rs. 12 lakhs, Analytics employees earn Rs. 14 lakhs,
Operations employees earn Rs. 9 lakhs, and Finance employees earn Rs. 10 lakhs. Individual
employee salaries within a department may vary, but the departmental averages remain as
stated. At the end of the fiscal year, the firm distributed a total performance bonus of Rs. 55

contribution to the firm's total annual salary expenditure.

In the following fiscal year, the firm implemented a salary revision with the stated goal of
raising the average annual salary across the entire firm by exactly Rs. 1 lakh. The management
decided that this revision would be achieved solely by increasing the salaries of Finance
department employees, while the salaries of all other departments remained unchanged.

A subsequent internal audit revealed the following: if exactly two employees were to be
transferred from the Finance department to the Strategy department with their individual
salaries remaining unchanged, the average annual salary of the Strategy department would
increase by Rs. 2 lakhs, while the average annual salary of the Finance department (after the
